speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, October 20, 1983 consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motions Nos. 41, 42, 43 and 46 (Mr. Benjamin), Motion No. 44 (Mr. McKnight) and Motion No. 45 (Mr. Mayer).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) had the floor at the adjournment of the House. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo).

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to speak on this series of motions which to some extent give a pretty fair indication of the effect of 12 to 40 years of Liberal bureaucracy in that this Bill before the House is so badly drafted that a number of things must be changed to even make it palatable and understandable.
This series of motions deals with sanctions and awards which may be levied by the Administrator. As you mentioned, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) was the last speaker and he gave a very interesting series of Bills which he thought should be presented to the House. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, because I would like to add to those Bills Conservative Bill C-112, which is a Bill that says that if a patient loses his hand the Conservatives would treat the heart because the darn thing is pumping out all the blood. That is the kind of inadequacy which we see in this whole series of amendments.
The intent of Motion No. 41 is to give to the Administrator the authority to make sanctions against the railways but not against the Wheat Board and other agencies of the Government. It, along with Motion No. 42, should be in the Bill to give authority to the Administrator to do his work properly and not be bothered with fighting with other agencies within the Government. For instance, Clause 21(1 )(a) requires the Administrator to establish performance objectives. Motion No. 42, which stands in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), attempts to reduce the confusion which
has been built into the Bill by bureaucrats who have become sloppy and did not bother to take a good look at the effect of the amendments. This particular amendment is an attempt to get rid of some of the confusion which is manifest in the Bill by allowing one agency of the Government-the Administrator, who is defined as an agent in the Bill-to levy sanctions against another agency, that being the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Grain Commission. It also attempts to strengthen a portion of the Railway Act.
Sanctions against the railways have been in the Railway Act for a great number of years. Unfortunately, the Canadian Transport Commission or the Government of Canada, the Cabinet, which has the power within the Railway Act to apply sanctions to the railways and force them to carry grain or whatever railways are built to do, has never used that power.
Motion No. 42 strengthens the Railway Act by giving the Administrator, this one-man agency, more power. He probably has more than he should but if he uses it well in forcing the railways to do their duty, it could be of some value. This amendment would allow the Administrator to have the sole responsibility for imposing sanctions on the railways. We recommend the amendment to both the Official Opposition and the Government as one way of assuring that we have the kind of control over the railways which, along with Motion No. 41, would guarantee performance. Since the Railway Act has not guaranteed performance although it has had the authority for many years, if we are to have an Administrator let us use him to develop the transportation of grain in such a way that it will not be affected by the dilatory railway.
Motion No. 43 deals with awards to system participants. It would eliminate the Wheat Board from the structure of a group that could receive awards because that particular idea of paying awards to a Government agency-again, one agency paying awards to another agency-does not have a great deal of logic to it. I suppose it could be considered to be incompetence on the part of the people who drafted the Bill. We suggest a change by taking out the railways as receivers of awards. They do not need awards. We have been giving the railways awards for the last 100 years and it has not improved their ability to do a good job.
Railways do not really need awards and the awards we have given them in the past have not produced good performance. We have given them rehabilitation funding, money for the rehabilitation of cars and rail lines. That can only be considered an award. Monetary awards have been given in the case of branch lines particularly, but the Government has never checked to see if the money was used for rehabilitation

of rail lines. What they did was take what little of the money was spent on the rehabilitation of that line and just added that money to their income.
That is the kind of award which the railways have been receiving and it has not made any difference in the quality of their service. A lot of awards in the form of hopper cars have also been given to the railways. The responsibility for the movement of grains belongs to the railways, according to the Railway Act and according to our understanding of why the railways are there. If one was driving a truck, for instance, one would expect to own the truck. One would not expect the Government to supply the truck even if one were moving Government goods. However, for the last number of years we have been supplying hopper cars and the railways have not been charged for that: they have been able to use those hopper cars rent free, so to speak. That must also be considered an award to the railways because they do not have to provide railway cars to move grain, as they did before 1950.
Motion No. 43, Mr. Speaker, also establishes the principle which Hon. Members have been speaking about for a number of weeks. The Wheat Board should not be tampered with. The second part of this amendment deals with the possibility of sanctions. Again, we feel that if sanctions were put in place they should not be levied against the Wheat Board, because any levy against the Wheat Board is a levy against the producer, and if we levy against the producer we are going to affect the cash flow of the producers. That is not the intent of this Bill. Consequently, we feel that this particular amendment should be allowed.

I would like to say at the outset that this will come back to haunt the Liberals for many years to come. The dismantling of the Crow rate will long be remembered on the Prairies. The Government, of course, will make much about the unwillingness of Hon. Members on this side of the House to join with it in its plans to scrap the Crow. Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, if you would give me a chance I am coming to the amendments we are discussing.
This group of amendments, Mr. Speaker, deals with the authority of the Administrator of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee to set performance objectives and a system of sanctions and awards to enforce those objectives. We agree that performance objectives should be set by the committee, but what is missing in this legislation is a restriction of its authority to set those objectives only for the railways. As I pointed out the other day when I was commenting on Motions Nos. 36, 37 and 38, the problem with our grain delivery system is not that the producers cannot get the grain to the elevator in time or that the grain is held up unnecessarily in port; the problem is and has been for quite a while that the railways cannot seem to meet their obligations to move grain quickly and efficiently from the country elevators to port. They have been responsible for millions of dollars worth of prairie grain sitting in cars on sidings by country elevators when it should have been at the port terminals being loaded on to ships for export.
I have been told horror stories, Mr. Speaker, about railways leaving full cars sitting at country elevators for up to 90 days. No doubt about it, we need to set performance objectives for the railways and make sure they meet them. But why, Mr. Speaker, do we need to have the Senior Grain Transportation Committee set performance objectives for the Grain Commission or the Wheat Board? Why do we need another regulatory body overseeing the other regulatory bodies which are responsible to their own Ministers? I think the simple answer is that we do not. In fact, as I pointed out the other day, allowing the Administrator of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee to interfere in the operation of the Wheat Board will weaken the Board's ability to market western grain. The intent of Motion No. 41 is to limit that interference.
Motion No. 42, Mr. Speaker, recognizes the simple fact that the railways have been at the public trough for long enough
October 24, 1983

now. By all means, set performance objectives for them, and if they do not meet those objectives, impose sanctions. But why in heaven's name do we offer them rewards for meeting their performance objectives? They have been taking the Canadian public for a ride for too long now. Let's make this the end of the line for the railways' public gratuities. Already this Bill proposes to hand over to the railways some $650 million annually as a Crow subsidy. The Government will be investing billions in upgrading our grain delivery system, much to the delight, no doubt, of CN and CP. If that is not enough, add to that the billions of dollars provided over the years in subsidies, the provision of grain hopper cars and deferred income tax. No, Mr. Speaker, the railways are already being rewarded handsomely for a pretty poor record of meeting their commitment to move grain quickly and efficiently to port.
If this Bill is allowed to pass through the House as it is now written, the railways will be rewarded again by the elimination of the Crow rate. However, this time the reward will be coming out of the pockets of prairie farmers. As far as I am concerned, the railways have gotten enough. It is ludicrous even to consider establishing a system of awards to be applied to CN and CP simply for meeting their performance objectives and doing their job. As David Lewis said many, many years ago, it is time to stop. It is time we cracked down on these corporate welfare bums and on corporate welfare handouts.
I would like to close, Mr. Speaker, by dealing briefly with Motions Nos. 45 and 46. These motions are very similar. Both increase the maximum sanction for the railways to 20 per cent of the volume-related variable costs. However, our Motion No. 46 goes one step further. For that reason, I believe it is the motion that we should support.
In addition to the 20 per cent of volume-related variable costs, this motion would make the railways liable to sanctions equal to 100 per cent of the capital portion of line-related variable costs on grain dependent branch lines. This would simply take from the railways all of the reward money the Bill gives to them if they do not meet their performance objectives or, in other words, if they do not do their job and indeed obey the laws that they are currently required to obey under the Railway Act.
Taken together, I think these sanctions would present a sufficient incentive for the railways to live up to their obligation to transport grain which they have been so delinquent at living up to in the past. It is high time that the railways started doing their job.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a few words on the record dealing with the motions that are lumped together here, Motions Nos. 41 through 46 inclusive. I would first like to say that I disagree with the fact that the motions are lumped together. Although they are similar in some respects, I would like to debate each of these motions separately because they do have separate intent and they are separate motions. It is very hard to say what we would like to say about all of these motions in the ten
Western Grain Transportation Act
minutes allowed. There are six motions lumped together and we do not have adequate time to cover each and every one of them as we would like to.
I would say initially, Mr. Speaker, that under Bill C-155 the railways have been given a guaranteed annual income. They are guaranteed a return of 20 per cent on their investment and they will either drain that out of the pockets of the farmers of Canada or, if that amount is more than the farmers can bear, they will drain that guaranteed annual income from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada through the Government of the country. I do not know of any farmer in my riding who would not be very happy to have a guaranteed annual return on his or her investment of 20 per cent. Things like that must be rectified.
The guaranteed annual income to the railways is not really tied to any performance indicators. If there are to be performance indicators, they should be set out in Bill C-155. In terms of the motions that are before us now, it would be very appropriate to have performance indicators spelled out within some sections of the Bill.
The entire system may be well managed, but if the railway companies do not perform and if performance indicators are not included and we cannot tell whether or not they have been performing, they should not have a guaranteed return on their investment of some 20 per cent. I will grant that it is not always the railway companies that are at fault. There are some situations in which the railway companies have performed very well. That usually happens on the main lines. The rail companies hardly ever seem to perform well on the branch lines.
The performance indicators, Mr. Speaker, should not only be tied in to the hauling of grain at a certain rate or with a certain turnaround time but should also take into account the fact that the rail companies have been responsible, or should have been responsible, for keeping the rail lines in an adequate condition so that they can be utilized to the fullest possible extent. This certainly is not the case. Performance indicators should be tied into the upgrading of the rail system.
I can think of situations where there is a need for hopper cars at delivery points with large grain storage capacities and yet there are only 85-pound steel tracks going into those places. The provincial Governments, the federal Government and the Canadian Wheat Board actually bought the grain hopper cars that the railway companies did not buy. Those cars should be able to go into delivery points where they are needed and be fully loaded and hauled back out. Of course, if there are only 85-pound steel tracks there, we all know that a box car can only be loaded one-third full and must be hauled out of that delivery point. That is a very inefficient kind of system.
I think that efficiency should be tied in to the performance indicators that the railway companies should be compelled to honour. Under the Act by which the railway companies operate, they are responsible for providing that service. They have received more than adequate compensation over the years for providing that service, either through land, cash grants, rolling stock or money to upgrade the rail systems. The railway

October 24, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act companies have not upgraded the system. They have let it waste away. Some of the tracks are in very poor condition. The railway companies have taken the money that should have been used for upgrading the rail system and spent it on numerous other things that have nothing to do with grain transportation.
That brings me to another point I wish to discuss, Mr. Speaker. Many things that are included in Bill C-155 should be debated separately. Bill C-155 has become known through the media to many farmers in western Canada as the Crow Bill. However, we know that the Bill deals with more than the statutory rate that is tied to the movement of grain. The Bill also deals with the upgrading of the rail transportation system and the leasing of the Dominion coal blocks. If the Bill were to be split into these three very separate issues as has been requested by Members of the New Democratic Party, Motions Nos. 41 through 46 would in fact fall under the section that would deal with the upgrading and improvements to the rail transportation system because the network that we presently have sometimes operates efficiently along main lines but very seldom operates with any degree of efficiency on branch lines.
As I have already said, while the cars may belong to the railway company and it can move them in, it is sometimes unable to move fully loaded cars out because of the condition of the tracks. Of course, track condition is a responsibility of the railway companies which should be taken into account in their performance. There is no way they should be allowed a guaranteed annual income of 20 per cent on their investment if they do not perform the movement of grain in the best interests of the producers. We have already heard about the Administrator's acting in the best interests of the producers for such things as trucking grain from certain delivery points. A conflict of interest may well arise if rail line maintenance is not tied into the performance indicators for the railways, because if they do not upgrade the rail lines and truck the grain instead, they would effectively kill that line and would have reason to go to the Canadian Transport Commission and ask for the abandonment of that rail line. Therefore I believe the branch lines are an integral part of the performance indicators of the railroads to justify their guaranteed annual income which is to be provided through this legislation.
Motions Nos. 41 through 46 deal with the power which is given to the Administrator, power which no individual should have. As I understand it, the Government wants to make the Administrator the sole person to solve all the problems of grain transportation. That person would be responsible to the Cabinet. These motions attempt to have the Government consider the fact that the Administrator should not have the power of sanctions and other means over the Canadian Wheat Board, which is a producer organization. The Wheat Board is a farmers' organization which performs in the best interests of producers in western Canada. Instead, the Administrator should be concerned with operating a more efficient grain transportation system in the best interests of the producers. We maintain that this should not be done by abandoning
branch lines, trucking grain and having power over the Wheat Board.

Mr. Speaker, there are presently six motions before the House. All of them seek to amend Clause 21 of Bill C-155. I consider those motions very important because Clause 21 of the Bill gives great discretionary power to the Governor in Council. In other words, that discretion is given to the Minister in charge of administering Bill C-155.
I would ask all Members of the Government to study Clause 21 of the Bill very closely. I say this because, having sat in this Parliament with my seatmate from Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) for some 15 years, we have seen Bills passed through the House of Commons, some of which we have supported and others which we have opposed. We have often seen the intent of legislation change quite drastically as a result of the regulations that are drafted by the Government itself or by the particular philosophy of the Minister in charge of a Bill. The reason for that is that a lot of discretionary power is given to the Minister in charge of a particular piece of legislation. He or she may interpret a Bill in any number of ways.
The six amendments in question today amend Clause 21 which gives the Minister tremendous discretionary powers regarding sanctions and awards to the participants in the grain handling system. Clause 21 states that the Governor in Council may, by regulation, at any time after the completion of the review that the Minister is required to carry out under Section 59, take a number of steps which are listed in that clause. This includes awards and sanctions as are detailed in Clause 21 (b)(i) and Clause 21(b)(ii) to be applied to the system participants. It goes on to talk about more regulations. Clause 21(3) states that the Governor in Council may make regulations establishing a system of arbitration to resolve disputes concerning awards or sanctions that are to be applied according to this legislation.
This clause gives tremendous discretionary power to any Minister. I say to my Liberal friends across the aisle that the time will eventually come, perhaps very soon, when they are not in Government and another Minister will be sitting across the way. I say to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) that the time may come when there will be a Minister other than one from his Government in charge of administering Bill C-155. That Member may then experience the same kind of frustration over the bureaucracy and lack of freedom of information one finds in the executive council in our country today. At that time he may wish that some amendments were passed to curtail the power of the Minister with respect to awards and sanctions on the grain handling system.
October 24, 1983

That is the thrust of the amendments that are before the House this morning. Our amendments and those moved by the Conservative Party attempt to limit the power that the Minister will be given through Orders in Council to draft regulations regarding sanctions in the grain handling system.
1 repeat that I seriously recommend to Government Members that they take a very serious look at Clause 21. If they did so I am sure they would be very interested in supporting some of these amendments in the name of democracy and fairness.
Let me refer specifically to Motion No. 41 which was moved by the Hon. Member for Regina West. That motion points out once again that we are dealing with a transportation bill and it should be treated as such. Motion No. 41 refers to the power to impose sanctions and we say that this power over the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain companies should not exist in this Bill. The Canadian Wheat Board is responsible to the farmers of this country and we believe that the Administrator and the Minister in charge of the Bill should not have the power to impose sanctions on the Canadian Wheat Board.
In reality, the sales that are made by the Canadian Wheat Board will determine grain transportation objectives. Therefore the Canadian Wheat Board, as the farmers' agency, should be able to allocate the cars to where it knows how much and what kind of grain is needed. I maintain that the Wheat Board and not the Administrator of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee should have that power.
The Hon. Member for Regina West, who has done a very commendable job on this Bill before the House, also moved Motion No. 42. That motion seeks to limit the application of sanctions to the railways for failure to meet performance objectives. There are a number of reasons why I would like to recommend this motion to the House. This part of the legislation would give the Administrator power to impose sanctions on the Canadian Wheat Board. We find it very absurd for one agency of the federal Government to be able to impose sanctions on another agency of the federal Government. In other words, the Minister in charge of this legislation can be given the power to impose sanctions on the Wheat Board, which is under the authority of Senator Argue in the other place. I do not believe it should operate in this way and the farmers of western Canada believe it should not operate in this way.
In the past it is only the railways which have consistently failed to meet performance requirements. I believe the sanctions need only apply to the railroads. The farmers for whom the Canadian Wheat Board is working should not have sanctions imposed upon them.
Motion No. 43 is also in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West. Once again it talks about the possibility of sanctions and awards being removed when it comes to the Canadian Wheat Board. The appropriate place for that amendment, as indicated in Motion No. 43, is once again in Clause 21. I do not want to repeat the arguments. We have said many times that sanctions must not apply to the Canadian Wheat Board, to grain companies, to the Wheat Pool and the
Western Grain Transportation Act
like; they should apply to the railways. There are many good reasons why that should occur.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Very simply put, our sole purpose throughout the discussion of the amendments to the changes the Government is proposing to the Crow rate has been to protect the interests of producers. When we talk about protecting their interests, one of their interests is costs. In that regard we have advanced the notion or the proposal of a three-year freeze on the rate charged to producers. The other area is that of guaranteeing service by the railways when it comes time for producers to move grain. In that regard Section 262 of the Railway Act protects producers, in fact all shippers, so that the railways are obligated to provide certain kinds of service.
This particular piece of legislation allows for another way that producers can be guaranteed protection. According to the Bill as drafted, a large amount of money will go to the railways each year. One way to put pressure on the railways to provide service is to take some of that money and hold it back, not for foolish or capricious reasons, but for reasons related to the performance of railways in the movement of grain. Motion No. 45 would amend Clause 21(2), which reads:
The sanctions referred to in subparagraph (l)(b)(ii) shall, in respect of any railway company, consist of a reduction in the government payment to the railway company under Part III, as prescribed by regulations made by the Governor in Council, not exceeding an amount that, in the opinion of the Commission, is equal to 10 per cent of the volume-related variable costs of the railway company.
To put that in perspective, about 80 per cent of the total amount of money the railways say they need to move grain is comprised of volume-related variable costs. If we take 10 per cent of 80 per cent, it means we are holding back 8 per cent of the Government money which will go to the railways. Let me emphasize that 8 per cent is not the amount which will be held back. It is a maximum, it is a variable. It is up to 8 per cent.
Motion No. 45 simply indicates that the Governor in Council should be in a position to hold back more. We are suggesting 20 per cent. Twenty per cent of 80 per cent is 16 per cent. That is not a large amount of money compared to the total. It is not an absolute, it is a maximum.
Just to give some figures, in 1983-84, if we use the 10 per cent figure, it would be $65 million out of total railway revenue of $790 million. In 1984-85, according to the figures provided by the Department, it would be $71 million out of $893 million. In 1985-86 it would be $75 million out of $987
million. Motion No. 45 simply suggests that that amount be doubled so that the railways know the Government is serious about seeing that they live up to their performance objectives.
In many ways it makes sense because producers do not have the option of receiving any of that Government money themselves. It all goes to the railways. If there was a provision in the Bill that some of the money would go to producers, they would then be in a position themselves to judge whether the railways were providing service. If the railways were not providing service and they had the option of using trucks to move some of their grain to a feed mill or crushing plant, they could do that. But when all the money the Government is to put up-and it is substantial, we give the Government credit for that-goes to the railways, surely there should be as many teeth in the Bill as possible to ensure that the railways perform. The amendment suggests that 8 per cent of the total amount of money is not enough and that 16 per cent would be more appropriate.
Let me put it further into perspective. As the Bill is written, volume-related variable costs will go down. There is a provision in the Bill that the railways be allowed a contribution to what is called their constant costs. As constant costs become a larger and larger proportion of the total amount of money that the railways will get from the Government, the actual percentage that is volume-related variable costs will decline. Over a period of time, the 8 per cent that the Government is suggesting in the Bill as it is written at report stage will decline. Over time the contribution to constant costs that the railways will be allowed to charge will amount to about 20 per cent. This becomes rather involved statistically and I am not sure it is worth elaborating. The point is that over time this 10 per cent figure will fall. It is now only 8 per cent and over time it will fall to less than 8 per cent.
If the Government is really serious about providing the producers of this country with some guarantees that the railways will in fact perform, there should be nothing wrong with doubling this holdback, which is all it can be termed, from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. Initially, the Bill at second reading was written to hold back 40 per cent of the^volume-related costs. Forty per cent of 20 per cent would only amount to 8 per cent of the total costs. As it is written now, it is raised to 10 per cent. A more reasonable proposition would be that it be doubled.
I am making these arguments to try and convince Government Members, but I do not know whether many of them are listening. Let me emphasize that the 20 per cent holdback is not a maximum. We are not saying that if the railway does not perform anything that does not come up to standard as judged by the CTC or the Governor in Council, the total amount should be held back. We are saying that the maximum should be raised. This was referred to by the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). Subclause (3) reads:

Where a scheme that provides for awards or sanctions or both has been implemented under subsection (1), the Governor in Council may make regulations-
It does not say "shall penalize" for the full 10 per cent or, as I am suggesting in this amendment, 20 per cent. It states:
-may make regulations establishing a system of arbitration to resolve disputes concerning awards or sanctions or both applied under the scheme in accordance with any procedures prescribed by the regulations.
If there is any faltering as far as performance is concerned, it does not say that the railways shall be penalized a full 20 per cent. All we are doing is raising the maximum. It does not mean that if there is a holdback or penalty it should be taken away permanently. As I interpret it, it means that the Governor in Council should be in a position to hold back certain amounts of money for a period of time until the railways perform. If the Government is really serious about seeing that the railways perform, given the fact that they are going to get many many hundreds of millions of dollars from the Government, the Government should be willing to see that there are some teeth in this Act in order that the railways do perform.
Let me point out another area of concern. In press releases last spring, both railways pointed out that because of the decline in the economy and the falling volumes that they were shipping, they may or may not invest the kind of moneys that they had initially talked about in the spring. Here we have an indication from the railways, and it makes sense because volumes are down, that they may not invest.
I will say this again so that Government Members in fact understand what Motion 45 states. We are saying that the Government should have as many teeth as possible to look after producers. Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on Motions Nos. 42, 43, 44, 45 and 46. It appears that these sections of the Bill are designed to protect the producers. That is certainly a worthy objective. These amendments deal with sanctions or penalties which may be imposed or enacted.
1 have difficulty following the argument that one segment of all those concerned is fully responsible for many of our problems. Certainly the railways play an important part, but there are other segments which also play an important part in transportation, such as the Wheat Board, the pools, the labour unions, the Canadian Transport Commission and the Grain Commission. All of them have their place.
Under this Act, the Administrator will be given certain authority. Some people, such as the Members of the NDP, think that the Administrator is being given too much authority. Frankly, I do not think he is being given enough authority. I would like to see it increased rather than decreased.
My experience with the abandonment of rail lines, for example, has not been a happy one. I was very unhappy with

the decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission. 1 tried to get information pertaining to the books of CPR and CNR. Not only was I thwarted by the railways, which did not want to reveal what was in their books, but by the CTC. In other words, the producers are being opposed by the very bodies that should be protecting them.
I want to give an illustration of that. It deals with penalties and sanctions. In the East Coulee coal mines, there are still more than a million tonnes of coal to be mined. A few years ago, the Canadian National Railway was persuaded to build a line from Rosedale to East Coulee, a distance of about eight miles. There were five coal mines there at the time. They paid for that rail line. When it reached the point where the coal mines could not compete with oil, the mines were closed. They stopped operating. The rail line and the elevator in East Coulee sat there. The CNR and CPR asked for the right to close the line. First, the Alberta Wheat Pool sold the elevator. The railways then said they did not need the line any longer. The railway companies produced a lot of figures at the hearings to indicate that the line was costing them money. Among other things, it showed depreciation on the line.
I knew that in fact the railways had put no money into that line for several years. However, they showed a large sum of money for depreciation. At the hearing, I asked the railways to show me the amounts of depreciation for each year since the railway was built. Counsel for the CPR said that I was not entitled to that information. I wanted to know why. After all, that was one of the factors upon which they were closing the line. CP said that it would not give me the information. One of the Commissioners of the CTC said that he believed I had the right to have the information. I almost fell over when he said that, but he did state that he believed I had the right to it. A very able lawyer in the City of Drumheller, Mr. Robert Ross, Q.C., supported me in the stand and stated: "Yes, he is entitled to that information. We are all entitled to it". The Commissioner then said to the railway representatives: "You supply the Member with that information".
I waited for weeks and for months and then I went back to the CTC and wanted to know why I was not getting the information that the CPR had been ordered to give to me. By that time the CTC had changed its mind and said: "We do not think you are entitled to that information".
I ask Hon. Members of this House, are the books of one of the segments going to be kept in such a way that the rest of us are not going to be permitted to see what is in the books? Why am I not entitled to see what the railway has been charging for depreciation on that line since its inception? I will warrant you, Mr. Speaker, that they have paid for that line time and time again through depreciation alone, but they will not reveal any figures.
I think we need an Administrator who is able to say: "We will look after the producer. We will look after the people. We want that information". If the railway is not giving the facts and refuses to give the facts, then there should be heavy

In navigation school where we were learning how to find the location of a plane, we would take a shot on the sun, we would take a shot on a station, and we would build a little triangle to find exactly where we were going to be in ten minutes. At night we would take a shot on a couple of stars and the moon, and we would get our little triangle to find out where we are so that we can tell the pilot, "This is where we are now. Mr. Speaker, in committee the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and some of my colleagues in the Conservative Party endeavored to have changes made in those parts of Clause 22 and Clause 25 which

specified the number of Senators or Members of the House of Commons who would need to sign a statement in writing requesting referral of the regulations put forward by the Grain Transportation Administrator to the appropriate committee of the House and, further, that when the committee had reported back, the report could be debated for three sitting days as proposed by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) or, as I propose, until debate is concluded.
In Motion No. 47 we endeavored to provide equality with Senators in terms of the number of Members required to sign a request to the Speaker that a regulation be referred to the appropriate standing committee. I can understand why they did not want 30 Senators and 30 MPs as it would be tough enough to find even 15 Senators to sign a piece of paper. We do not object to 15 Senators but we think only the same number of Members of the House of Commons should be required to sign a submission in writing to the Chair that a regulation be referred to the appropriate standing committee of the House.
As was the case with the previous group of amendments and as was mentioned by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), this legislation is another VIA Rail set-up. The Governor in Council, the Minister, or the Grain Transportation Administrator can do anything they want. When it comes to regulations regarding awards and sanctions, regulations regarding the allocation of railway cars, regulations that could affect the quota system or the block system or regulations that could discriminate against a system participant unfairly or discrminate in favour of a system participant unfairly, it surely requires some detailed attention by the House of Commons. The regulations will be contentious and they are to be submitted to the House by the Minister within five days. There will probably never be a request that those that are minor or somewhat innocuous be referred to the appropriate standing committee for debate.
It can be safely assumed, however, that there will be many regulations of a very serious and complex nature that cannot be grasped quickly and so will require the attention of Members both in the standing committee and in the House. We submit that it is only fair that an equivalent number of Members of Parliament as members of the other place can make a request in writing.
I will not go into any criticism of members of the other place except to say that it seems to me and to this Party that Members of the House of Commons have the greatest responsibility to go into these matters because every day they have to face the people who sent them here and give an accounting of what they are doing. Certainly Members from western Canada will be called upon to explain the regulations put forward by the Minister if this legislation should ever pass.
With regard to Motion No. 48, the Bill asks for a one-hour debate consisting of ten-minute speeches in the House. We can all see of course that some complicated, serious and important regulations will need more than one hour of debate. The limit of one hour of debate with ten-minute speeches is a sort of legislated closure-it legislates time allocation in advance. I

Motion No. 49 standing in my name leaves the matter open. Where there are contentious regulations, and when those committees report back to the House, the opportunity should be there for the House to debate those regulations fully. .We believe this time allocation in advance with respect to an area such as this is totally inappropriate and we would urge that the Government reconsider and accept our Motion No. 47. Members of the House of Commons that we be treated equally in the matter of numbers with the other place.
Secondly, the Government must surely agree that limiting debate on such regulations to one hour is unfair. There might be the odd minor regulation for which an hour would be sufficient; indeed, an hour might not even be used up. However, there will be other regulations, Mr. Speaker, which will require lengthy debate, because when those regulations are being dealt with by a standing committee of the House, there will be representations from one or even all of the system participants affected under the legislation. There would be representations from governmental bodies which are not, strictly speaking, a system participant but are affected by the regulations. If a regulation allowing some kind of variable rate system in a specific area jeopardizes the existence of some branch lines, you can be certain, Mr. Speaker, that the municipalities in that area will want to be heard and the provincial Government will want to be heard. They can be heard before the committee if the committee will agree to call witnesses, if the committee is authorized to call witnesses, and the committee should be authorized to do so. However, once that stage has been completed, then the House requires more than an hour on those kinds of contentious regulations in order to debate their efficacy and whether or not they should be changed or amended. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and to commend him on his foresight in proposing the adoption of this amendment to the House. I hope Government Members opposite will pay attention to this particular amendment because I believe it is crucial to the future of grain transportation and other product transportation in western Canada.
It is wise, I believe, to track through this entire piece of legislation to see what brings us to this particular amendment. What we have before us is a piece of legislation which is trying to help Canadians look into the future to see how best to regulate and encourage the railway system to become more effective and efficient, and to enable Canada as a nation to better our capacity to deliver our export products on time and at a reasonable price.
Mixed in with that, Mr. Speaker, is the notion that a Cabinet of this House of Commons shall decide regulatory matters. Built into the proposed law, Mr. Speaker, is a principle whereby 10 per cent of the Members of this House of Commons can petition the House to have a one-hour debate on a particular regulation. Is a one-hour debate reasonable, Mr. Speaker? I suggest that it is the firmly held view of Members of the Conservative Party of Canada and Hon. Members of this House that a one-hour debate is simply not reasonable. We are not dealing here with something which is simple to discuss, nor are we dealing with regulations which will have very little impact on the lives of Canadians. We are dealing with regulations which will have an enormous impact on the lives of Canadians, particularly those in western Canada.
If one looks at the current constitution of the federal Cabinet, Mr. Speaker, it is wise to note, I believe, that there is not a single elected Member west of the Manitoba border. There is only one elected Member from the Province of Manitoba. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there is simply the one voice of one Member in the Cabinet of Canada who is accountable to the electors of western Canada. That Hon. Member is city born and, perhaps, more attuned to eastern Canada. With respect to his past performance over four years, it is hard for me to distinguish him from someone who was born and raised in the City of Toronto in terms of his attitude.

Is it reasonable, Mr. Speaker, for that very, very busy group of people who constitute the Cabinet of Canada, those 37 individuals of whom only one is accountable to the voters of western Canada, to make decisions which so profoundly affect the lives of western Canadians? Is it reasonable to provide in this piece of legislation the possibility for only one hour of debate in this Chamber on a regulation which might have the impact of bankrupting 100 per cent of the agricultural producers in western Canada, or 2 per cent, or 10 per cent, or 50 per cent? The only protection which those producers in western Canada would have through their elected representatives is the possibility of a one-hour debate in this Chamber. We know, Mr. Speaker, what happens to one-hour debates in this Chamber. The Government uses its majority to use up 30 minutes of the 60 minutes and we are left with the possibility of only 30 minutes worth of time for the elected representatives from western Canada to be heard about a regulation which has the potential to make life very difficult for producers.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the Cabinet of Canada would promulgate a regulation of that kind if it had knowledge of the potential impacts of that regulation. However, I do suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that given the busy nature of Cabinet Ministers and the fact that we will occasionally have Parliaments which are heavily weighted to other regions of the country, where there is only one elected voice from western Canada sitting in the Cabinet, the odds of that Cabinet inadvertently making a decision which would have a profound, long-term, negative impact on the economy of western Canada are very, very high.
It is a wise Government, Mr. Speaker, and it would be a wise group of Government backbenchers, which would look closely at Motion No. 48. It protects the Government against itself. It protects a busy group of Cabinet Ministers from making a tragic mistake in regulations which would cause them considerable grief over time because it would cause large numbers of Canadians considerable grief over time.
What we are saying to the Government, Mr. Speaker, is that when 10 per cent of the Members of this Chamber petition this House to debate a proposed regulation, then give the elected representatives an adequate amount of time to represent their constituents and inform the Government and Cabinet about the potential negative impact of any proposed regulation on the economy and the farmers of western Canada.
The only reason 1 can see for the Government insisting on the one-hour limit is stubbornness, a declaration to the Canadian people that the Government and Cabinet of Canada is not willing to learn about the potential impact of a proposed regulation. Why else would the Government insist on restricting Opposition voices to 30 minutes on an issue which might involve hundreds of millions of dollars and affect hundreds of thousands of Canadians? These regulations could affect Canadians' lifestyle today and their future retirement. Surely those kinds of very important considerations deserve up to
Western Grain Transportation Act three days of the time of this Chamber solely for the purpose of allowing elected representatives to bring to the attention of the Government that by supporting a particular regulation at a particular point in time the Government is in danger of making a tragic mistake.
Thirty minutes or even 60 minutes is not sufficient time to deal with the kinds of complex issues existing in Bill C-155 and the regulatory powers therein. Three days is not a great deal of time but in our view it would be sufficient. The Government would be free to make its mistake but it would do so with knowledge rather than with ignorance. I urge Members opposite to support the Hon. Member for Vegreville and vote yes for the adoption of the amendment under Motion No. 48.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly to Motion No. 48 and in so doing, since the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) talked about the prospects of several regulations being debated as a group, I thought it should be pointed out that Clause 24(1) of the Bill provides:
A regulation made under subsection 21(1) shall be laid before each House of Parliament within fifteen sitting days after it is made.
(2) Within five sitting days after a regulation referred to in Subsection (1) is laid before either House of Parliament, a motion to the effect that the regulation be confirmed, signed by a Minister of the Crown, shall be filed with the Speaker.
The word "shall" was incorporated in the committee hearings. Then we get into Clause 25(1) which provides:
A motion filed under section 24 shall be taken up and considered by the Senate or House of Commons, as the case may be, within five sitting days after the filing of the motion.
Then this is where Motion No. 48 standing under my name comes into effect. Clause 25(2) provides:
A motion taken up and considered in accordance with Subsection (1) shall be debated without interruption for not more than one hour, during which time no Senator or Member may speak for more than ten minutes-
I think when the Hon. Member for Regina West was speaking to this group of motions he indicated that this motion was reasonable. 1 would have to agree with him. I think it is a fair compromise. His argument for the open-endedness of this particular provision is that his motion would not provide any time limit. In general I agree with that, but we are really not dealing with legislation here, we are dealing with a regulation. The provision in this Bill for the possible debate of a regulation is something not often found in legislation. So it is a step in the right direction.
While I have no argument with the hon. Member's Motion No. 49, I thought that because we were dealing here with a specific regulation, not a group of regulations, three days was certainly a lot better than one hour. I think the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) elaborated on that very well.
In this Bill putting a great deal of latitude and discretionary power in the hands of a number of people, particularly the Administrator and others charged with the responsibility of administering the grain handling and transportation system. In the course of our deliberations we tried to incorporate as many of the players as possible, particularly the producer; but the

Western Grain Transportation Act
bottom line is that sooner or later regulations will have to be made and this provision is, in principle, a commendable check and balance which I certainly support and agree with. However, having said that, the Government certainly should provide sufficient latitude to do the job well.
In my humble opinion, to debate a controversial regulation in one hour certainly does not fit the Bill. My view is that non-controversial regulations would naturally not be brought before the House for debate; but clearly if one is important enough to be brought before either House for debate, there should be sufficient latitude and provision for debate to take place in full. Perhaps three days is not enough, but it is a happy compromise and, I think, reasonable. So I hope Government Members seriously look at Motion No. 48. It goes some way in alleviating some of the concerns which could crop up, and I concur wholeheartedly with the comments made by my colleague from Calgary West. As one who is not happy with any kind of allocation or predetermined time limit, I think we have gone some way in meeting an objective of fairness and reasonableness and I commend Motion No. 48 to the House for support.

subsubtopic: LEBANON-BOMBING FATALITIES SUFFERED BY UNITED STATES AND FRENCH FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope that I speak for all Members in this House when I say that words are inadequate to express the feeling of horror and dismay that surged through all of us over the weekend on learning of the savage and unprovoked slaughter that occurred in Lebanon during which upwards of 200 American and French servicemen died in their sleep under the rubble of buildings that were heartlessly demolished in a sneak attack on their barracks.
The American, British, French, and Italian forces are in Lebanon for one purpose only, namely, to provide negotiating time so that the contending forces in that war-weary and faction ridden country can work out their differences and produce a durable solution.
That shameless, senseless, and subhuman attack can only set that process back. Those responsible will have to bear the total burden for their iniquitous behaviour in destroying defenceless men, because they will inevitably call down on themselves the retribution they so richly deserve. I think that this House will want to send its condolences to the families of those victims.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS AT DOMINION BRIDGE PLANT IN WINNIPEG
LAY-OFFS AT DOMINION BRIDGE PLANT IN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to speak on a serious matter of loss of jobs at the Dominion Bridge plant in Winnipeg. This plant laid off another 65 workers in mid October. This western plant has manpower facilities, capacity, ability and experience to fulfil transmission tower line construction contracts abroad.
Several weeks ago Dominion Bridge of Winnipeg submitted the lowest of four Canadian tenders on a $7.5 million transmission line project in Pakistan under our CIDA program. As soon as the contract is awarded, many of the laid-off workers would be eligible for recall as this project is expected to provide 65 man-years of work. I urge the Minister responsible to expedite the approval and signing of this contract without further delay.

Madam Speaker, today the doors of Native Friendship Centres from coast to coast are closed to protest delay in delivery of funding for the new Native Friendship Centre Program which was approved by Cabinet on May 13, 1983. In front of 60 Friendship Centre representatives in Vancouver on May 29 of this year, the Secretary of State announced that the new program would come into effect April 1, 1983, and would run for five years.
The present Native Friendship Centre Program encompasses a network of 84 Friendship Centres, six developing centres, their provincial and territorial associations, as well as a national office. This well thought out and excellent Program is designed to improve the quality of life for native people in an urban environment, and it provides such services as employment counselling, legal information, emergency shelter, youth programs, alcohol counselling, family counselling, and others.
The delay in delivery of this negotiated program has caused centres to incur thousands of dollars in bank interest charges and has brought many to the brink of financial collapse. The success of Friendship Centres in assisting native people to adjust to mainstream society is recognized by all levels, including Cabinet. Therefore it is unacceptable that the Government should now go back on its word and jeopardize this most worth-while program. Funding, as promised, should be provided immediately.

Madam Speaker, today is United Nations Day. We would do well to remember the purpose of the United Nations which was set up to create a system for the maintenance of international peace and security. To that end a set of principles was drafted for the conduct of states. Chief among those principles is the commitment not to use force in international affairs, and not to interfere in other states' domestic affairs. Those principles are as valid today as they were when the UN Charter was drafted in 1945.
But we need only look around us to recognize that every citizen of every nation must redouble their efforts in support of those principles. Today, there are some 45 states, one out of every four nations, at war. More than four million soldiers are directly involved in those wars, and between one million and five million people have been killed in them. Today we should be mindful of that.
We should also be mindful of the threat to international security posed by the rising tide of terrorism. Yesterday's senseless bombing in Beirut, which has now claimed more than 170 American lives and more than 40 French troops, all assigned to Lebanon on so-called peacekeeping missions, is only the most recent and most graphic example. Our condemnation of terrorism must extend to the attacks on Corinto and

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is now 50 years since the first recorded holocaust in the history of mankind, and the largest holocaust of this century. It preceded the Jewish holocaust by some ten years, and was possibly its precursor.
To those who survived it, it is known as "the great famine", or "the great artificial, man-made famine". Between 1932 and 1933 some six million to ten million Ukrainians in the rurai areas of the Ukrainian-Soviet Socialist Republic were systematically starved to death. Those responsible for this crime were never brought to justice, and the Soviet Government has done everything in its power to remove any evidence relating to this horrifying deed.
On behalf of those Canadians of Ukrainian origin and, indeed, on behalf of all Canadians, I urge the Government of Canada to propose a General Assembly resolution at the United Nations calling for an independent inquiry to determine who was responsible for the holocaust.
To date, based on the studies mostly of Ukrainian scholars, survivors, their relatives, and on a few reports of correspondents of the time, the Soviet Government of that era is the obvious prime suspect. Crimes of such magnitude against humanity must be investigated by judicial bodies of international stature to establish legal identification of the perpetrators. Only then could public opinion in free nations be harnessed to strengthen further human rights legislation and its enforcement to prevent further such horrendous crimes.

Madam Speaker, invididuals charged and convicted of brutal murder have been released on parole and have subsequently been charged with committing other crimes. I do not want to dwell on the specifics of any case, but I want all of us to think about our families, our children, and the citizens of the country, and wonder how much protection innocent Canadians really have.
I am an advocate of capital punishment to protect the innocent. I know capital punishment is not the sole answer to resolving the weaknesses in our justice system, but it is a major step toward protecting the innocent. I know it is difficult for some Hon. Members to accept that capital punishment is a deterrent to those warped humans who kill in cold blood. It is hard to understand what goes on in the minds of cold-blooded killers. However, I know, after being a police officer for six years, that with the reintroduction of capital punishment convicted murderers will not murder again.
The people of my riding have seen more than their fair share of brutal crime, and they speak with one mind on the issue of capital punishment. The majority of the people of Mission-Port Moody want to see the reintroduction of capital punishment for convicted first degree murderers. We, as lawmakers of the country, should heed this call.

subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EUROPE-ISSUE OF FRENCH AND BRITISH MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. On the weekend millions of people around the world were demonstrating for the cause of peace, particularly the cause of disarmament, concerned about the apparent deadlock that exists in the talks between the superpowers.
Last April I asked the Prime Minister if he thought any reasonable calculation of the balance of forces between the two great nuclear powers should include the French and British missiles. At that time the Prime Minister dismissed the question. Since then a number of European leaders, a number of former NATO generals, and Canadian Admiral Falls have said that the French and British nuclear missiles should be included in such calculations as a means of making a constructive proposal that could lead to some kind of settlement. Has the Prime Minister rethought this matter, and will he now agree that the French and British missiles should be included?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN EUROPE-ISSUE OF FRENCH AND BRITISH MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member asks if I have rethought the matter. I do not want to sound immodest, but I have been thinking of it for quite a few months. When he suggests that 1 dismissed his suggestion, I think the expression is perhaps incorrect. I do not remember the exact exchange, but even those who listened to rumours at Williamsburg will know that the question of counting the French and English missiles, at some point, in some way in some talks, is not unreasonable. 1 have said that on various occasions. Therefore, I am not dismissing it out of hand. I have not dismissed it. It is a very complex negotiation.
When we are talking of the INF negotiations in Geneva, I do not think it is right to contemplate including the British and the French systems, because they are strategic systems. They are not theatre, or they are not intermediate nuclear forces. They are considered by those sovereign nations as strategic forces and, therefore, the solution might be to count them at some point in the START talks but not in the INF talks.
I cannot speak for France or Britain. I do not want, as a NATO ally, to state any position which would not be agreed to by them. I know that for the point of view of the Germans, for instance, they cannot count on the French or the British nuclear arms because they are strategic arms used by those countries to protect their sovereignty. The Germans, who have no nuclear arms under their total control, have to count on the Americans.
It is not unreasonable for the Americans to say, "Well, we should have as much as the Soviets." If the Soviets say, "We must put the American, British and French in the same basket and we Soviets have equal to that total", then obviously that is a way for the Soviet Union to state that it must have absolute superiority over the United States. I do not think that even my hon. friend would want that to happen. Therefore, it is somewhat complex to make a bland statement about the French and British missiles.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister seemed to come down again on both sides of the street in this admittedly complex issue. As he knows, the largest mass based democratic party in western Europe, namely, the SPD in Germany, which to some extent can be regarded as the author of the two-track policy which the Prime Minister has given a lot of support to, is now, with its leader, clearly saying publicly, as are Canadians and Americans of some distinction, with considerable expertise in this field, that there ought to be such a calculation that takes into account the French and British missiles.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister to be a little more declaratory here today. He said there were rumours coming out of Williamsburg. He is usually the first to dismiss rumours. Would he now tell us if in the discussions that took place with President Reagan in particular he put forward, on the part of Canada, a package that included the counting of the French and British missiles? If he did not, why did he not?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Member has accused me of being vague and being on both sides of the street. I noted his words, "such a calculation", which would include the French and the British. I do not think that is coming down on both sides of the street; that is making a difference between INF and START. The Hon. Member, by using these words "such a calculation", put himself squarely on both sides of the street. I would like to know what he means by "such a calculation"?

If the Prime Minister from time to time would participate in the debates on disarmament in this House we would all learn very well where the Government stands. He should just do that, once in this House.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to present to the House of Commons today a petition signed by residents of my riding, particularly those from the centres of The Battlefords, Rud-dell, Vawn, Cochin and Cole Bay. The petition. Madam Speaker, was signed during "An Evening in the Park" which was sponsored by the Battlefords Association for Nuclear Disarmament and calls upon Parliament to debate and pass Bill-678, an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone, and thereby place the nation of Canada in a position to act as a mediator in the worldwide nuclear disarmament process.
