He said: Madam Speaker, I am very pleased, as events have turned out, that we have an opportunity today to give final passage to Bill C-163, to establish the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. I recognize that this proposal receives the full endorsement of all Hon. Members of the House, and well it should because it is very important step forward in putting in place good protection for the Canadian travelling public and advancing our ability to pursue safety standards in the country. In so doing, I pay tribute to members of the Standing Committee on Transport from all Parties who worked very diligently to deal with the matter. In fact, they moved it along with a great deal of dispatch and a strong sense of support.
The Bill itself contains several major changes which will ensure that aviation safety is both seen to be and will be a matter of high priority and in which the most adequate and effective form of investigation will take place. The first major principle of the Bill is in fact the establishment of a board to conduct all investigations and inquiries into any aviation occurrence. The importance of that is highlighted in the findings of the Dubin inquiry which pointed out the inconsistency of having the Minister of Transport being responsible for the rules and regulations on safety and for investigating any
Canadian Aviation Safely Board
infraction of those rules. It is like being judge and jury at the same time.
The Bill will set up an independent board that will be able to work in an arm's length fashion from the Department of Transport and therefore be in a position to deal with any aviation accidents in a very open and clear manner without any sense or perception that somehow it is a matter about which the Department of Transport, the Government or someone else is trying not to provide all the facts. The independence itself is a very important matter.
The second major result of the Bill will be to ensure that inquiries and investigations will make public recommendations so that there will be no apprehension on the part of the travelling public or of any other member of society that something is being held back. In fact, the Bill gives the Safety Board the right to hold public inquiries and to request the Governor in Council to set up such inquiries under the Inquiries Act.
I am sure Hon. Members will know that just two weeks ago I established a public inquiry to look into the Gimli air accident where, because of the unusual circumstances surrounding that particular problem, there was a high degree of concern on the part of many people about follow-up disciplinary actions and the questions of culpability and responsibility. Therefore, a public inquiry was called which took an exceptional initiative. We had to clear it through Cabinet and take unusual action. The establishment of this Board will no longer require that to take place. The Board will have the authority to hold public inquiries or to initiate them. In itself that is a major improvement.
While the Board itself will be a three-person board, it will have a full range of experts to call upon to work on its behalf. Therefore, it will be able to offer a very extensive and comprehensive examination, assessment and judgment on any aviation occurrence. I want to make this clear because some questions were asked in committee and also in the Senate prehearings concerning its range, whether in fact it would involve matters dealing with search and rescue questions. Of course it would be in a position to examine aviation-related matters and would cover a widespread concern relating to air incidents.
Under the provisions of the Bill it would be my hope that we will be able to identify clearly the causes of many of the occurrences or incidents and have them reported so that we can prevent accidents. Unfortunately, we are too often in the position of responding after a tragedy occurs.
Also, under the provisions of the Bill the Air Safety Board will be in a position to have a clear monitoring responsibility or reporting responsibility so that if it begins to detect a pattern of problems occurring, it will be able to act before the tragedy occurs and to recommend to Government, to other agencies or airlines the necessity to change a technique, a pattern or a behaviour in order to prevent the occurrence. On that basis we hope the Safety Board will be able to act before the fact rather than after the fact.

October 24, 1983
Canadian Aviation Safety Board
Further, this Bill by its very definition deals with matters of aviation safety. That is a clear response to the Dubin inquiry. However, the Government does not intend to stop there. We recognize the necessity of setting up similar kinds of improvements in other modes of transportation. Hon. Members of the House will know that we presently have the Deschenes inquiry in the maritime area. I asked the Commissioner of that inquiry to see whether it might accelerate certain of its findings so that we will perhaps be in a position to take further action in the maritime area on the safety issue, whether it be a matter of melding it into this Board or whether it be a separate board. After discussions with Mr. Deschenes, he agreed to attempt to move his study forward at a faster pace so that perhaps we will be in a position in a few months to bring recommendations forward to the House and therefore to committee for further examination in the maritime area and to provide a full and comprehensive approach to the problems in transportation safety.
I do not think 1 have to argue this Bill at third reading. Since it is accepted, I will simply reiterate my appreciation for the support given to it by members of the Standing Committee on Transport. 1 endorse it to the House and to the Senate, so that we can get on with the business of ensuring that Canadians will be safe when they travel.

Mr. Speaker, sometimes it is difficult to step into a debate quickly, as we have to do this afternoon, and try to express in a very few moments the feelings of all my colleagues on a Bill as important as Bill C-163.
I want to commence my remarks by making a few references to the Hansard of this House over the past few weeks. Something has happened which I frankly find quite distasteful in reference to the Bill. For example, on September 19, the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) said, as reported on page 27247 of Hansard:
-there is a bill to establish a new air safety board presently before the Transport committee. If the Opposition were to co-operate we could get that legislation through very quickly and into the House so that we could have a proper mechanism under which public inquiries could be undertaken.
The next statement to which I want to refer is reported on page 27765 of Hansard for October 5 where, in answer to a question during Oral Questions put by the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), the Minister of Transport said:
As soon as the Opposition is prepared to pass it, we will be in a position to bring forward the aviation safety Bill.
Then, on October 20, as reported at page 28193 of Hansard, in reply to the Hon. Member for Peterborough in the adjournment debate, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) said:
The Hon. Member might also speak to his leader because such an occurrence would be investigated by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board under Bill C-163. However, we saw in the House the despicable behaviour of the Official Opposition filibustering Bill C-155. Therefore we cannot bring in Bill C-163. We have an all-Party agreement to put it through the House quickly.
All three of those quotations are frankly, and colloquially, a crock.
This Bill was instigated initially by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) when, as Minister of Transport in the Thirtieth Parliament, he asked that the government inquiry deal with matters of safety in the air transportation field. After that report came in, the then Minister of Transport, now Secretary of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), started the process to bring the Bill before the House.
He, as was his wont, confided with the members of the Standing Committee on Transport in the fall of 1982. While he may have been speaking in confidence at the time, there is no point in not repeating the fact that he told us that the Bill having to do with the Canadian Aviation Safety Board was ready and he was looking forward to an opportunity with his House Leader to get it before the House of Commons. Some months later, earlier this year, after a great deal of negotiation and pleading on our part to have that Bill brought before the House, finally the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) allowed it to be brought before the House on the second or third last day of June. We, as we had promised to do, passed it through the House rapidly. As I recall, we sent it to committee that very afternoon.
Unfortunately, there was a bell vote. The Committee could not finish its deliberations. We were unable to complete the deliberations on that Bill in committee prior to the House shutting down for the summer recess. On very short notice, we had appearing before us the President of the Canadian Owners and Pilots Association as well as the General Manager of that Association, the President and one other member of the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association and the senior executive officer, 1 do not know whether it was the President, of the Air Transport Association of Canada and others of that type who where willing to give the Committee the benefit of their advice and counsel. They came on very short notice.
I should go on record to point out that the President, if that is his title, of the Air Transport Association of Canada returned, as did the General Manager of COPA to the Committee meetings in the fall. They indeed acted as expert witnesses before the Committee.
The Committee, and certainly this Party, dealt with this Bill in the most expeditious and responsible way that could be expected of any Party. Never at any point have we held this Bill up in any way, shape or form. While I am at it, I might point out that the Transport Committee, as it has in the past, dealt with the Bill in a very non-partisan way. We debated amendments and dealt with the Bill in a manner that would put it through as it should have been a long time ago.
The Bill is a pretty good Bill. It was made better by the amendments made in committee. I want to pay full tribute to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), who prepared a number of amendments over the summer. He submitted them to the Chairman of the Committee and the Minister and his staff. Some were adopted by the Committee. The Bill was made considerably better by the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East who has sponsored Private Members' Bills over the years and in other ways
October 24, 1983

attempted to get before the House the principle of a safety board, not only for aviation but for other modes as well.
1 am delighted to hear the Minister point out that we are now going to be dealing, to quote him, in an expeditious way with a similar safety board for the other modes of travel. His use of the word "expeditious", given the fact that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East has been asking for this legislation for a decade or better, is a bit of a contradiction in terms. Nonetheless, it is on its way.
As I said, the Bill is not bad. It was made better and could have been made better yet. I will refer only to two further amendments that were put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, both of which, in the opinion of those Members who sit regularly on the Committee, would have made it better. I stress that because, as happens frequently in committee hearings, a number of Government Members were brought in and asked to vote just as they were told about a subject they knew absolutely nothing about. That is a shame because the two amendments were quite straightforward.
In the Bill there is a requirement that the Board report to the House through a Minister other than the Minister of Transport. Again, my colleague for Dartmouth-Halifax East put in his amendment that the report should come through the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan).
The purpose was very clear and simple. It would seem quite illogical that this most important Board would report through, for example, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, the Minister responsible for Mines or some other Minister, important though they may be, but who know little if anything about the intricacies of this matter. Therefore, to have this Board report through the chief law officer of the Crown, the Minister of Justice, because it deals with legal matters, seems to be entirely sensible and reasonable. 1 do not understand why it would be rejected.
Frankly, for a moment I thought about attempting at this late point to ask for unanimous consent to repeat a request of a Member of the House. I think, with his consent, I will not now do so. The Bill is that far along that we will see it through this afternoon. I am sure the Member would agree with me that while the legislation would be better and the results would be better by having his amendment in place, nonetheless we would rather have the Bill pass with this one fault than not have it pass at all. We will not take the chance of not having it passed. The amendment was very simple. I will not read it in detail, line after line.
The amendment was simply that any witness appearing before the Canadian Aviation Safety Board would have the right to the protection of the Canada Evidence Act. It is very simple, half a dozen words, but it has a lot of meaning. A great deal of stress was put on this in the Committee by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) and others who felt that these few words in the amendment would have given people appearing before the Board a safety factor that they do not now have. It would take time, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, to see exactly what will happen. I guess the only
Canadian Aviation Safety Board
thing we can say is that, slightly flawed as it is, we would rather see the legislation go through knowing that a few months down the road we will have an opportunity to act as a Government and, if we see that it is necessary, we can put an amendment in place at that time. At that time, Mr. Speaker, they may well agree to it.
There is little need for further comment on the Bill. The Bill is, as I said, the result of years of effort on the part of the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East. It is the result of the definitive effort of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) as a former Minister of Transport. We have, indeed, taken too much time now to bring that Bill to fruition. I am delighted that we finally have it. I hope that, given the kind of co-operation that we always received in the Standing Committee on Transport, we will have the opportunity soon to implement much of the balance of the Dubin inquiry report.
I cannot resist, Mr. Speaker, putting a plug in here for a document on domestic air carrier policy that was prepared by that same Committee on Transport. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) and my colleague for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) in speaking on third Reading of this Bill.

evening all summer, all fall and some of the spring. We did, in fact, function in the evening when the House was not sitting.
On this legislation, as my colleague for Prince Edward-Hasting has said, there was a determination by Members to achieve speeds parliamentary action on instituting legislation for the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. There was no disagreement on the principle of having such an institution. There was disagreement on some particular parts of the Bill; some were resolved by amendments and compromises. I suppose I could also say I am happy to see this Bill going through because crows are part of aviation. I might want to have some aviation safety board hearings on the crows that might get shot down if another Bill passes.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Committee, the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings, the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister of Transport for accepting my amendment. There are two others they did not accept, but I guess nobody is perfect. The one that they did accept is welcomed, with a great sigh of relief, by the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association, the Air Traffic Controllers Association and the Canadian Association of Pilots and Owners. It was not the objective of the Aviation Safety Board to apportion any blame or liability in connection with aviation occurrences. After meeting with the officials and discussion in the committee we came up with the revised wording. I was assured by the officials and we agreed in the Committee that the wording would meet the objective that I had in mind with my original amendment.
There is much confusion about the words "occurrences, incidents and accidents". An occurrence can be merely that, or an occurrence can be an incident, or an occurrence can be an accident. Concern was expressed by those involved in the aviation industry-again I am thinking of the pilots, the air traffic controllers, the flight attendants, the Pilots and Owners Association, the Canadian Air Transport Association-that the purpose of an aviation safety board is not only to investigate an accident, an occurrence that is an accident, or an occurrence that could lead to an accident. This is where I had some difference of opinion with my colleagues in the Committee and with the Government officials. It is the responsibility in law of the Department of Transport and its air transport committee to investigate occurrences that could lead to an accident or an incident that would be dangerous. It is also its responsibility to look into the efficacy of regulations. My experience has been in another mode of transportation years ago. Certainly what employees in the aircraft industry, the aviation industry, the marine industry and other transportation modes have said is that too often there is a tendency on the part of either a Government or a corporation to do what is called "scapegoating".
There have been three or four incidents and accidents involving Canadian commercial aircraft in the past year or so. I do not want to interfere with grievances that might be going on between the Canadian Air Line Pilots' Association and Air Canada or any other grievance, but all this indicates to me that people are still looking around for someone to blame.
When I worked on the railway, Mr. Speaker, there was a mishap about ten miles away from where I was working and the chief dispatcher sent me over to handle train orders and such things. The section foreman at my place of work who handled about 15 miles of track, in three different years had been awarded the prize for having the best section in the whole 600 or 700 miles of track in the Medicine division. Every spring he would plead and beg and ask for enough new ties, rails, rail anchors, spikes, ballast, weed spray and other things to keep the track in a safe operating condition. Every year his requirements were cut back. Although he had been awarded the prize for the best kept section in the division, when that accident occurred in the snow and rain in April, there were eight carloads of grain in the ditch-two of them contained flax which at that time was worth about $3.50 per bushel- and after it was all over, that poor section foreman received 30 or 40 demerit marks because of a broken rail. That man never missed a day of work. Every time a train went by he followed it and inspected the track. Even on Saturday and Sunday when he was off duty, if there were extra trains, he would follow them. He got demerit marks. Still, he was blamed for not finding the broken rail. It did not matter that every year he had begged and pleaded for new rails, or complained that some of the rails in use had been made in 1905 or 1910.
Quite often the causes of transportation accidents, in this case an aviation accident, can be traced back to those who are in charge and have the final responsibility-the place where the buck stops. The pilot who saves lines while his aircraft is out of fuel deserves a medal; he does not deserve to be taken out of the service.
If the regulations governing training of ground crews and refuelling are not enforced sufficiently and properly, then mistakes will occur somewhere down the line and some poor pilot or some poor kid holding a jet fuel hose on the tarmac will be the victim. I submit that the Aviation Safety Board should follow matters up the line to determine who goofed in not making sure that everyone was fully aware of his responsibility and that he carried out those responsibilities so there is no scapegoating when we have a terrible occurrence, and aviation accident.
I appreciate the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings about the Canada Evidence Act. The failure of the Government to include that is going to leave the Government open to lawsuits down the road. It seems to me that two things will happen if the protection of the Canada Evidence Act is not available. First, some of the legitimate efforts of the Aviation Safety Board will not be carried out because witnesses who could shed light on the matter will be less than forthcoming, or not forthcoming at all. The Minister should have an amendment made when the Bill goes to the Senate. When it comes back to the House we will deal with it in an hour or two; there is no problem about that. But without the protection of the Canada Evidence Act, if a witness is forthcoming fearful of being blamed and ends up being or found liable even in part, I suspect he will go all the way to the
October 24, 1983

Supreme Court; not only on account of the Evidence Act, but on account of the Charter of Rights.
The purpose of a Canadian aviation safety board is not only to find out causes, why an accident happened, but to determine the chain of events, without laying any blame or assessing any liability, so that subsequently the courts or the lawyers for the parties concerned can assess matters and arrive at agreement, or the courts will settle the matter. I submit that that should be the limit of the work of an aviation safety board.
There may be incidents, such as near misses involving aircraft separation. This is where there may be some duplication of the legislation. The Department of Transport and the Air Transport Committee could be looking into occurrences and incidents that do not necessarily end in an accident. The whole matter of aircraft separation and ground movement on an airport while air traffic movement is going on is a concern. There was a problem about that recently. In the end, the Ministry of Transport has responsibility, and the legislation requires an investigation of occurrences that are incidents or occurrences that do not result in an accident in order that any deficiencies in the regulations or training, or whatever, are corrected, and corrected promptly.
The difference between the authority of the Department of Transport and the Aviation Safety Board is the difference of time. An aviation safety board may take months or years to arrive at conclusions, whereas investigations of incidents and occurrences-as was set out in the amendment that the Government did not accept in committee-are the responsibility under law of the Department of Transport and the air transport committee of the CTC and can be dealt with much more quickly. They can be very minor things, but they can be dealt with in a matter of days or weeks. The effect could be something like preventive medicine. If an Aviation Safety Board takes upon itself the investigation of an occurrence that did not result in an accident-and it can under the legislation-I submit that will do nothing more than give the Department or the CTC an excuse or may compel them to delay making a decision.
That is the problem with the duplication of effort that will occur as a result of the law as it stands and the provisions of the Bill. I hope that those who administer it and those who serve on the Aviation Safety Board will not be in conflict. I hope they will confine themselves to the area in which they are best qualified to act upon and to report on. If that is accomplished, Mr. Speaker, then we have done some excellent work with this legislation, because of the trauma a whole nation feels when there is an accident, whether or not there are any lives lost. A number of my colleagues and myself attended the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association Conference in New Zealand in 1979 when the DC-10 crashed at the South Pole. That whole country went into trauma. It was widespread around the world, but in that country itself the soul-searching and agonizing has gone on ever since. What did we do wrong? What could we have done to prevent that from happening? A piece of legislation like this, Sir, is important to the whole matter of safety for every nation.
Government Organization Act, 1983
I believe the laws of this nation are very deficient in railway health and safety practices, in highway health and safety practices and in marine health and safety practices. It took years to get survival suits for sailors on vessels sailing in the wintertime in the northern climate of Canada. It was to give these men a chance to survive and perhaps allow them to survive a few hours in cold water, and the years it took to get that done is no credit to this Parliament or this Government, and no credit to those who owned the ships and did not want to do it because it was too expensive.
We must do whatever is required with this legislation and the law as it already deals with transportation. When it comes to health and safety you cannot put price tags on the lives of people, whether it is a customer or an employee. The more we can do as a country to maximize safety and, more important, the prevention of accidents, whether by air or any other mode of transportation, the better we are as a society and the better we do as a Parliament.
I hope that the Minister of Transport will reflect upon the work of the Committee on this legislation and on other pieces of legislation. Perhaps he will allow the Transport Committee to consider Bill C-155 for a few months. He might then find himself with some legislation which will be acceptable to most of those affected by it.
We are prepared to support this legislation. I hope the Minister will ask the Senate to consider the amendment mentioned by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings regarding the Canada Evidence Act, so that there will be no delay. The Senate can then return it, we can deal with it in an hour or so, and the Bill will be much improved.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.

I will accept the fullest responsibility, if any, with regard to the deletion of Clause 25 of the Bill because that is a different matter.
Let us look at the purport of Motions Nos. 1, 3 and 7, which have to do with the title of the Minister for International Trade. Clause 4 of the Bill says a Minister for International Trade shall be appointed. This is a mandatory requirement in the House that we should have a Minister and he shall assist the Minister for External Affairs in carrying out his responsibilities relating to international trade. Therefore, he is a Minister appointed to assist another Minister in carrying out a
October 24, 1983

portion of what you might call Canada's external relations. That is the trade side. Then the Minister of International Trade has certain responsibilities which may be given to him as they appear in Clause 12 of the Bill at page 4. But here there was an amendment introduced in committee, which met with unanimous consent, that Clause 12 would be subject to Clause 6 because:
A Minister appointed pursuant to section 4 or 5 shall act with the concurrence of the Minister in carrying out his responsibilities and shall make use of the services and facilities of the Department of External Affairs.
This is in effect taking the trade commissioner service and all those aspects of trade out of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and merging them into the Department of External Affairs. There will be an under-secretary of state for external affairs who will be the senior deputy minister. Then there will be the appointment of a person of a deputy minister rank who will be in charge of the administration of international trade. He will have the rank, I suppose, of an associate under-secretary of state for external affairs, to keep the title in the same sort of wording.
Then we have another appointee who is going to be called a Minister for External Relations, and that has to do with those amendments which appear in Motions Nos. 2 and 8. But he has no direct responsibilities except to assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs in discharging those duties which may be assigned to him by the Minister. This is what we have seen in practice. The Minister of State for External Relations is here in Ottawa and he becomes the spokesman for the Government on an international matter, non-trade, in the event the Minister for External Affairs is absent from the country or incapacitated.
In addition, the Minister for External Relations can also be a spokesman for the Minister for International Trade in the event that that individual is absent from the country, incapacitated or unable to speak on behalf of the Government. If the Minister for External Affairs is not able to act, for whatever valid reason, it is the Minister for International Trade who shall be senior in the Department and Acting Minister for External Affairs.
This was explained to the committee in some detail. However, strangely enough, there has been an odd choice of people for the jobs. The man who presently occupies the position of Minister of State for External Relations is the number three man in seniority in the Cabinet. In the absence of his Minister, who happens to be the Deputy Prime Minister and number two man in seniority in the Cabinet, it is the Minister of State for External Relations who speaks over his colleague, the Minister of State for International Trade, who would otherwise have spoken. That is one of those little accidents that occur in the combinations of seniority on the Privy Council list and the so-called seniority of the pecking order of that Department.
This combination has been going on for some time. As a matter of fact, we know that in Canadian posts abroad, the

titles of the Ministers, 1 believe we are dealing with those amendments at this time. I will deal with the reason for the change that has occurred in the titles of Minister of State for International Trade and Minister of State for External Relations.
Although the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) and the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) will have identical powers as Minister of State, they will still be Ministers who assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). The purpose of identifying them as such and creating these positions through a new Act rather than through the Ministries and Ministers of State Act is to provide a higher international profile for these Ministers. That is precisely the purpose for the change.
If the Hon. Member considers the Bill very carefully, he will see that the powers of these two Ministers are restricted to those powers granted to Ministers of State even though they are not called Ministers of State. They will have a higher international profile and a higher profile within the configuration of the Department of External Affairs. That is why the titles were changed. The Hon. Mr. Speaker, I would be glad if the Hon. Member would respond. If I may say so, and I expect the Hon. Member will agree with me, the Parliamentary Secretary has missed the point the Hon. Member was making.
As we in the House have pointed out previously here and in committee, one of the great anomalies in this Bill is that whereas the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has a deputy minister under him, the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) does not. In fact, the administrative chart indicates that the Minister of State for External Relations is hanging in limbo. We will deal with that in more detail when we reach the next two motions.
We understand the reason for this technical change in the title of Minister of State to Minister. There is no question in our minds about that. We also understand why the post of Minister of State for International Trade is a post that shall be created whereas the post of Minister of State for External Relations is a post that may be created. I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary needs to worry about our understanding of these particular amendments as we have spent a very great deal of time on them in committee.
1 first addressed the larger problem in the House on June 22 of this year, as reported beginning at page 26,705 of Hansard. In the case of the grouping of amendments, the problem is
whether or not the Government made a wise decision when it decided to break up the old Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and put the industry part in the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion and put the trade part in External Affairs. As the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, we are not too sure where the domestic commerce part will be put, but it will probably be put in the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion. Unfortunately, that is now a fait accompli.
I do believe that the reorganization which has resulted in this Bill was the brainchild of the former Secretary of the Privy Council. The Cabinet simply found it difficult to unravel this incredible creation that he had made. It will probably take the Department years to try to accommodate itself to these reorganizational changes as is quite clear when one examines the most recent chart issued by the Department of External Affairs.
With respect to attempting to combine trade with external relations, it will have two consequences. I simply want to repeat those consequences but not dwell on them today since it is a fait accompli and not much can be done about it. The first consequence of separating industry from trade is that the trade side is deprived of its clientele, so to speak, which is the industrial base in Canada. When the two were together one could examine the export performance of Canadian industries in particular and relate that directly to the trade needs and expectations of the Canadian Government. While trade commissioners were under the authority of External Affairs in their missions abroad, there was a very tight link at home between the people involved with trade and those involved with industry. Some of us fear that this linkage, which is so essential to the development of Canadian export industries, will be lost in this reorganization, and that industry, which is currently under the Department of Regional and Industrial Economic Expansion, will be narrow and inward looking rather than in the broad and outward looking tradition of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Indeed, I can remember when the Department of Industry was first created as a separate Department from Trade and Commerce in approximately 1964. It operated that way for a few years until it was recognized to be more desirable to combine industry with trade and commerce for the very reasons I have given.
Now, as a result of the elaborate ideas of the former Secretary of the Privy Council, they are separated again. In my opinion it is a mistake and will be shown to be so as this unravels.
There is a second reason why some of us are concerned about placing the Minister of State for International Trade essentially within the Department of External Affairs to assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). Rather than being a separate Minister in the Cabinet, we have a fear that trade orientation in the Department of External Affairs could possibly take over from orientation on policy and political matters, which is so crucial in all foreign policy
October 24, 1983

discussions and decisions. Indeed, the Minister of State for External Relations appeared before the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. He was asked before the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. He was asked if the message from this departmental reorganization was that our External Affairs would be much more dominated by trade orientation- although I think it will be unsuccessful-to which the Minister said, "Yes, that is the message."
Some of us would have thought that it would have been far better to leave trade and commerce with industry where it was operating quite satisfactorily. There were close links at the mission level in the field with External Affairs. If we wanted to give a particular message in foreign policy terms, it might have been more desirable to have a Minister assisting the Secretary of State for External Affairs in such matters as arms control and disarmament. I suggest that could have been the type of additional policy thrust that could be used and, in my view, should have been used.
These points have been raised before and I have already indicated that there is almost no further point in talking about them because this is a fait accompli. Since the reorganization is under way I can only hope that when it comes time for the Committee to discuss the performance of the new Department we will have more clear charts of the organizational structure so that we can better understand it and have a clearer picture of the process of integration that all of this reorganization is supposed to achieve. While we are skeptical at the moment, we hope that at least within a year there will be something good to say about this particular reorganization, and specifically on these motions in relation to the Minister of State for International Trade.

Mr. Speaker, this is of some interest to members of the Committee and I rise to speak on this Bill because Members who were on the Committee know that this Bill has been the subject of some conversation in Committee. I hesitate to correct the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) but it is important to realize, in understanding this, that the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) does not have a deputy minister for international trade. There is a deputy minister for international trade who does not report to him but in fact reports to the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), as was pointed out a moment ago by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. I will come back to his remarks because they reflect the nub of this issue.
To bring Members up to date let me say that some time ago the decision was taken to merge international trade with External Affairs. That decision has been taken and the reorganization has taken place. As the Hon. Member who preceded me stated, it is a fait accompli. In fact, when we were dealing with the diagrams with regard to this Bill at the committee, we discovered that the diagrams were out of whack with the Bill. The Government had to amend the Bill to bring it into conformity with the diagrams it was already circulating to its employees. This meant quite clearly that we were dealing with an administrative event after the fact. Let us accept that because we accepted it at committee.
When we were asking the question why we were changing the status of a Minister, it became very clear that there was more to this than the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary suggests. As the Government proposed, there was not to be a department of international trade within the Department of External Affairs, as there could have been, with the Minister at its head. There were some who believed that that was the streaming that made sense in order to preserve the integrity of the trade officers and the trade commissions. However, the Government, in its wisdom, chose not to do that but to make the whole thing report to a three-headed ministerial group, one of whom shall be the senior Minister and two of whom shall be junior Ministers. Quite reasonably, the Government used the Prime Ministerial power of appointment of Ministers of State to say that there shall be two Ministers of State under the Prime Minister's authority, one for international trade and one for external relations.

Government Organization Act, 1983
That is when the problem arose. I should explain that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has the right to appoint, withdraw or change his Ministers of State at any time unless those Ministers of State have status in law as the head of a Department under which the departmental authority is given to them by the House. We had two Ministers of State. The question arose as to whether the position of the Minister of State for International Trade could be abolished? The answer was that it could. Then someone wisely said that we had better come forward and obtain legislative authority to say that there shall be a legislative mandate stipulating that there shall be somebody-and I will come back to this in a minute-for international trade under the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Then we got the Bill indicating that there shall be-not may be-a Minister of International Trade. The proposed amendment suggests that there shall be-and that wording is important because it protects, as was intended, the guarantee that there would be somebody responsible for International Trade-somebody responsible in the Department. The amendment before the House guarantees that because we believe there should be somebody in the Department responsible for international trade. However, the Government went further than that. It did not simply say that there shall be a Minister of State but, rather, it said that there shall be a Minister. The argument made in committee, as was made here a few minutes ago by the Parliamentary Secretary, was that in the world at large there needed to be a Minister as opposed to a Minister of State.
The role of the Minister of State underneath the Minister is generally used in the world. In fact, if we look to our Mother Parliament, we find that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or the British equivalent, has four Ministers of State under him, all of whom are widely accepted around the world in the export development role, the trade role, the general bilateral role between countries and the expected multilateral discussions, whether they be for foreign affairs, trade or whatever.
Then we return to the question of why Canada was doing it. In other words, why were we being asked to change a Minister of State who had no Department, no authority or no people, into a Minister? There are two answers to that question, which go beyond the question of the international role of developing trade. First, the incumbent of the post of Minister of State for International Trade did not like being called Minister of State; he preferred being called a Minister. It was not an international issue; it was a domestic issue. However, the most important part, after reading the entire Bill, was that under the Salaries Act a Minister of State who does not have a Department, as is the case of the two current Ministers of State, is not eligible for or does not count in the creation of the post called "Parliamentary Secretary". I will deal with the section on Parliamentary Secretaries in a moment, but it is relevant to mention it for the time being. Ministers of the Crown count in the creation of the post called "Parliamentary Secretary". The maximum number of Parliamentary Secretaries which can be
created today is equivalent to the number of Ministers of the Crown.
The Bill proposes to say that the maximum number of Parliamentary Secretaries shall be the number of Ministers of the Crown, plus the number of Ministers of State who have Departments to administer. Lo and behold, someone figured out that neither the Minister of State for International Trade nor the Minister of State for External Relations would count in the Parliamentary Secretaries section because neither of them had a Department. In order to create two more Parliamentary Secretaries, the Government proposes to rename the two Ministers of State as Ministers. It does not change one whit, as the Parliamentary Secretary admitted a few moments ago, the status, power, ability or legislative authority of any of the occupants of the positions to call them "Ministers". It changes the capacity of the Government to add two more folks to the roster or the Government's payroll who will be called "Parliamentary Secretaries". Everyone who knows the House of Commons knows that we are desperately running out of Liberals who have not already had the plum. That is the only effect of the change as it is proposed.
I suggest that Hon. Members opposite should read the amendment very carefully because it is designed and written to meet the concerns of the Department and those concerned with international trade. It is reasonable that there should be the word "shall" in the clause on appointment in order to ensure that someone exists who is charged exclusively, if under the Secretary of State for External Affairs, with the responsibility for international trade development. This is absolutely essential to the future of Canada, but it is not important in terms of the administration or the law. It does not make any difference whether that person is called a Minister of State or a Minister.
Hon. Members opposite may or may not choose to rise to debate this point. I ask them to bring forward evidence, because none was presented before the committee, to refute it. We have asked repeatedly those involved in international trade whether the issue was a guarantee that there would be somebody named in the law, somebody who cannot be withdrawn by the Prime Minister, somebody who has been created by an Act of the House of Commons, to work exclusively in international trade, given that trade was being merged into external affairs. The answer has been, "That is what we want. If we cannot have a full trade commission, if we must accept the merger, at least give us someone responsible for trade".
In this amendment we are saying that there shall be a Minister of State for International Trade, but there does not need to be another Parliamentary Secretary and, therefore, there does not need to be a word change from Minister of State to Minister, a Minister who will have no staff or authority, save that delegated in writing and over the signature of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, no Department, no people to administer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not take part in the committee hearing, but I have heard what has been said this afternoon. I am amazed, with the television program from Great Britain, "Mr. Minister", having such
October 24, 1983

wide appeal across Canada, that the Government would suddenly create another Minister for no purpose. Can we imagine a Minister being asked, "What is your Department?", and the Minister saying, "Oh, I do not have one; 1 am sort of the runaround boy for the Minister", Who will say, "Yes, Minister"? Does the Minister say, "Yes, Minister" to the Minister's Minister? Where do we go?
This is an effort to add to the illusion of having a Cabinet Minister responsible for something when in fact we do not have a Cabinet Minister responsible for anything other than carrying the bags of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If that is what is intended, why does the Government not organize to have a series of Parliamentary Secretaries to assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs or, at the very most, a Minister of State to assist him? Surely to goodness to create another Minister who has no Department or direct responsibilities just so that he can be called a Minister makes no sense. That is what is being proposed by the Government in Clause 4 of the Bill.
Therefore, the amendment of my colleague makes eminent sense. We cannot go on forever trying to pretend that people are something they are not. The Government is pretending that it has a Minister in charge of international trade. Well, it does not. It has a Minister who is responsible to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It does not have a Minister for International Trade; it has a person who carries the suitcase of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he goes on a trip. It may be someone the Minister can send on a trip to represent him, but the person is really not a Minister because the person has no direct ministerial responsibilities.
I, for one, feel that the reorganization Bill is wrong. We should have trade commissioners who are responsible to a Minister of trade. Trade matters should be followed up separately and distinctly from matters involving diplomacy, peace, war and the rest. Trade is perhaps one of the most important things we can be doing. Efforts should be made to have a Minister in charge of international trade as well as a Department of international trade. We do not need someone following the Minister of External Affairs around the world, somebody who is not directly responsible. We need someone who is responsible for ensuring that international trade is conducted for the advancement of the affairs of Canada.
This is a hopeless system. We have a Minister, but there is no Department for that Minister. The Minister is to assist the Minister in carrying out his responsiblities relating to international trade. What kind of law is that? If we are going to have a reorganization of the Government, we should rethink the whole Bill. If we want the person in charge of international trade as a Minister, as he should be, surely he should be responsible for international trade and have a Department. He should be the Minister of International Trade.
That is not what is happening here. This person who is to be called Minister is not a Minister, but a batboy. He is somebody who will carry the suitcases. He does not have the right
Government Organization Act, 1983
to make a decision, he does not have a Department to direct and he cannot commit the Minister. He is to assist the Minister. He is an assistant or executive secretary.
That is not a Minister, and let us not say it is. Let us call him a Minister of State. There is nothing wrong with having Ministers of State. In fact, this is probably an excellent way of organizing the Cabinet system. Let us not get carried away by calling someone a Minister who is not a Minister.
As the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) said, the only reason for this is so that the Government can appoint an extra Parliamentary Secretary. Why have a Parliamentary Secretary for a Minister of State? If there is a need for additional help, surely that can be obtained. Perhaps we need more parliamentarians involved on the Government side. We should involve Parliament more often, but it should not be necessary to appoint a Parliamentary Secretary to a Minister who is not responsible for anything other than to carry the bags of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
All that has happened here is that the current Ministers of State involving external relations and international trade feel a bit slighted by being called Ministers of State. They want to be full Ministers. That is too bad. Is there any reason why we should change the legislation of Canada in order to come to grips with the personal problem of two Ministers who should be Ministers of State because that is the way the organization chart works?
The statute we are now debating is not to be debated because of the personalities of the two Ministers of the Crown. They are Ministers of State. If their obligation is to follow the directions given to them by the Minister of External Affairs, that is their obligation in the Cabinet system. In that sense they are Ministers of State. Let us not call them Ministers, because they are not Ministers. They are batboys or servants, but not Ministers.
In the organization of Government, we must determine what is meant by the designation "Minister" and what is meant by the designation "Minister of State". It has been that the Minister of State is a Minister who assists another Minister, a sub-Minister or assistant Minister, if you like. We have a Minister of State for Finance to assist the Minister of Finance. That is proper. It is perhaps the way it should be organized.
I have some difficulty with this, but if it is the Government's organization pattern, then there should be a Minister for External Relations or External Affairs and Ministers of State as may be required to handle the External Affairs portfolio. Perhaps two or three Ministers of State are required to assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs. After all, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is not very competent. We saw how competent he was in the Finance portfolio. Undoubtedly he needs a lot of assistance. He needs a great deal of help. There is certainly no call to have all of his helpers called full Ministers.
On that basis, it is totally wrong to follow through on the Bill in the way it has been presented. I commend to the House amendment No. 1 and the other amendments dealing with this

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to take part in this debate on Motion No. 1 in the name of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). The speakers from this side who preceded me have made the points very well. I will enter into the debate from the position of looking at other Departments. If you read the Bill, you will see that it states:
A Minister for International Trade shall be appointed-
The active word is "shall", not "as may be required". It states "shall be appointed". If that was standing by itself without the knowledge that we have of the Department and of the reorganization Bill, it would probably be an acceptable amendment. If the Government wished to create a Minister, it would imply that there would be a ministry. We could all accept that.
However, it goes on to say, "Shall be appointed by commission under the Great Seal to assist the Minister in carrying out". That refers to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If that is put in context, the amendment that stands in the name of the Hon. Member for Edmonton West turns that around and states, "A Minister of State for International Trade", not a Minister.
Most people in Canada consider that a Ministry includes a Minister. If you look at the reorganization chart for the External Affairs Department, you see a fairly solid line connecting the present Minister of State for International Trade, who under this Bill will become a Minister. If you turn it around and look at the other side of the Department and look at the Ministry of State for External Relations, it is a very thinly dotted line connecting that part of the Department of External Affairs to the External Relations Secretariat as it now exists.
Mr. Speaker, if you would like to draw another conclusion with other Government Departments that we see now, under the Secretary of State there is a Secretary of State for Multiculturalism, and under the Department of the Secretary of State there is a solid hiving off with officials and with responsibilities under the Secretary of State for Multiculturalism. As a matter of fact, that Secretary of State for Multiculturalism, included in the Department of the Secretary of State, has more power than the Minister for International Trade, who will be assisting the Minister of External Affairs in his responsibilities under this Bill. He has more power to act as a Minister, to sign on behalf of his hived-off Department than we see under this amendment. Bill C-152 says that there will be a Minister of International Trade created, but there is no Ministry for that person to become involved in.
I guess you could go two ways; either there is a Secretary of State for International Trade and that is all, or there is a full Ministry. But under the Government reorganization Bill it is neither chick nor fowl. We are half in and half out. There is
not the responsibility, there is not in this Bill a full Ministry, yet we are pulling a hoax, we are trying to prevent a Member on the Government side from having that power and being a full Minister.
What would happen if there was conflict? I think, Mr. Speaker, we are all aware that in international affairs there can occasionally be conflict between trade and relations with other countries in the External Affairs Department. If there is some point of recognition by the Government through External Affairs of some action which could jeopardize trade, who would carry the message for the trade side? Would it be, as in the Government reorganization Bill, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan), who really is just an assistant to the Minister of External Affairs, or if it were set up as a separate Ministry, would they argue as equal Ministers or, as it is under our amendment, would it be the secretary of state for international trade who, all in all, would then be recognized purely and simply as being an assistant?
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we can expect understanding and sympathy from the Canadian public when words really do not mean anything. Either a Minister is a Minister with a full Department or a Minister is a Secretary of State assisting another Minister in a Department. If we are going to be straightforward and factual, as in the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West, the Minister of State shall be called the Minister of State for international trade. There would not be any hoax. There would not be any use of words that misdirect people into thinking that there is a full Ministry behind the Minister for International Trade.
I hope that because the Government would like to represent itself as being straightforward so that there be no misunderstanding about its direction in this reorganization Bill it will accept the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West that the minister of state for international trade shall be appointed. When you say "shall" you are appointing a Minister without the full responsibility which most people in Canada expect from a Minister of the Crown.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few observations as well to the amendment put forth by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
Motions Nos. 1, 3 and 7 are an attempt by my colleague to bring some common sense to a proposed Government reorganization. Of course we know it is not going to be accepted in spite of the fact that it would be in the best interests of the nation and it makes sense, just practical, on the street common sense. It will never come about because the Government, the Cabinet, has decided it is going to be a certain way and it does not matter what any of the Opposition Members think. The Government will be backed by its Members who will not understand one bit of what this is really about but will stand and rise because the Cabinet made the decision.
We also know that the reason for the decision to call these two gentlemen Ministers rather than Ministers of State is
October 24, 1983

really simply to flatter their personal egos. Where you were once a Minister to be seen to become a Minister of State is an enormous demotion in your personal status and image. Therefore, the whole operation of the Government of Canada is going to be shifted around so that two individuals can "keep their egos intact".
What a ridiculous way to run a Government. Surely the bottom line should always be what is in the best interest of the nation. I think the evidence is clear from many, many experts in the field that you simply cannot weld all of that world of external affairs where you have to deal with individuals in foreign countries and you have to deal with all sorts of political ideologies. You might, as a matter of external affairs, need to take a position in your country that is quite opposed to a position that you might take in trade. For example, throughout many wars in the past, where nations as a matter of external affairs have been in a state of war, they have continued at a different level to operate in trade. With both of those functions being under the Minister whom we normally call the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he has the total and final responsibility to try to weld these two together. It simply cannot be done. That is why we argue.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenicarn) said that if we are going to go into this as a matter of principle we should have a separate Ministry for international trade. There are a lot of arguments to show that should be in place, because we are, as Canadians, a trading nation. We are a small nation with enormous resources. I think that most of our ordinary citizens genuinely do not appreciate the extent to which foreign trade brings wealth to this nation. Perhaps in the West we understand it because so much of our population is engaged in agriculture where the grain is exported directly. I would have thought that in manufacturing, most people working in plants, particularly the automobile industry, would realize that a lot of the automobile parts and cars are exported to the United States. At the grassroot level we do not seem to appreciate the fact that we are a tremendous trading nation and therefore surely that should be the most important of Departments.
What has the Government done? The Government has decided to make International Trade de facto a Ministry of State because all the powers and functions of the Minister responsible are the functions of a Ministry of State with no Ministry underneath, no departmental officials. Because of the ego factor we have to call them Mr. Minister so that they can feel important even though they do not have any Department. That is an incredible statement about the conduct of the national affairs of this nation by the Liberal Party and the Cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, this reorganization also shows the incredible departmental battles that go on below the Cabinet level of which most of us as individuals, even though we are elected here and attend committee meetings, have no idea. We had an example of that in the Canagrex battle where it was agricultural officials against IT and C officials. Unfortunately, again in that instance, Industry, Trade and Commerce lost the
Government Organization Act, 1983 battle. All their trade officers, who have done an excellent job in international trade, were lost. They lost the battle, and a new Crown corporation, Canagrex, was created which can put officers in the field. We have further emasculated the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and put the trade operation in with the Department of External Affairs. We are going to have an industry in Canada carrying on with no direct links with the trade function and the trade commissioners. At the same time, the Department of Agriculture will be operating on its own. We could have half a dozen officers in Tokyo all from different Departments and acting as agents for the Minister of State for International Trade, and none of them knowing what they are doing. There will be confusion and, as a result, export sales will be lost. I can say without fear of contradiction that within a few years, even months, we will be reorganizing that Department. When it costs us exports, it costs us jobs, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps then, when thousands more people are drawing unemployment insurance, the Government will respond and common sense will prevail.
If we had put this in the hands of half a dozen Members of Parliament and ignored the politics of it we could have found a solution which was far different from this one. The parliamentary task forces have shown that it is possible.
I hope the Government has listened carefully to the Canadian Exporters' Association which made the case, and very forcefully, that policy and trade cannot be mixed. That association is convinced that the officials in the field who should be signing the bottom line, will now spend their time developing papers to be sent back to Ottawa will be taken over by policy end of things. We will have to watch that very carefully but under the present structure, I think it is inevitable.
1 would ask my colleagues opposite to consider seriously Motions No. 1, No. 3 and No. 7, and not just follow the Government line. They should do what is right for the nation. It is clearly right for the nation that these people be called Ministers of State: that is what they are, de facto. Let us make them de jure what they are, de facto.

Mr. Speaker, last week in the House we had an example of an extraordinary situation of stumbling in precedence. The person who is third on the list in the Ministry is the Minister of State (External Relations). A question was put to the Minister of State (External Relations) (Mr. Pepin) which related to an external relations matter, namely the situation in Grenada. Up popped the Minister of State (International Trade) (Mr. Regan) to answer the question. The Minister of State (International Trade), is, at a rough estimate, about number 12 on the list of precedence. The Minister of State (External Relations) was in the House but he did not answer the question. The Minister of State (International Trade) answered the question on external affairs although the appropriate Minister, who is number three on the list of precedence in the Ministry, sat in his place and allowed the Minister of State (International Trade) to answer the question on international affairs.

October 24, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
I do not know whether this Bill is intended to sort out these anomalies and to clarify the situation with respect to precedence. As I understand precedence, it is arrived at by the date on which various members of the Ministry take the oath to become Minister. Therefore, I find it more than a little strange that number 12 on the list should override number three on the list and answer questions relating to a matter to which number three on the list would normally be expected to reply.
I suppose this whole thing boils down to the Bill before us to try to sort out the organizational mess in the Department of External Affairs by creating three Ministers-which is what the Bill seems to suggest is required-in order to run that huge Department. At one time there were something in the order of ten under-secretaries and assistant under-secretaries in that Department. About a week or ten days ago when I checked 1 found that there are 42 assistant under-secretaries or associate under-secretaries or deputy under-secretaries. Perhaps the creation of Ministers rather than Ministers of State is to give Members of Cabinet sufficient authority to keep track of and control these numerous members of the top echelons of the Department of External Affairs.
I know there has been a movement in the direction of integrating the trade commissioners service in Ottawa with the Department of External Affairs and getting the officers who have served abroad in the trade commissioner service under the same roof as members of the Department of External Affairs when they are at home. The purpose of this is not entirely clear to me. Having served a fair number of years in the Department of External Affairs, it was always my experience that members of the trade commissioner service were well integrated in the operations of the mission abroad. I can cite five, six, seven or eight posts in which I served where that was the fact. The reporting was done directly by the trade commissioner service to the Department of Trade and Industry. Through weekly meetings the other members in the post were made aware of the efforts being made by which the trade commissioner service abroad would find markets for our products.
Now we find that instead of remaining with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the trade commissioner service officers have been shifted, for administrative purposes in Ottawa, into the Department of External Affairs. We find that in order to look after their affairs in that Department, we need a Minister of State (International Trade) or, as this legislation suggests, a Minister for International Trade. Perhaps the problem, Mr. Speaker, is that the Minister of State (International Trade) is not able to control the trade officers who are under his jurisdiction and, therefore, he has to be a Minister. This triple Ministry-tricephalous is a good word- is a three-headed monster, if I can translate for your edification, Sir. The Department of External Affairs is a threeheaded monster. There is no shortage of monsters. A couple of them have been picked and now they want three of them, and they have decided they shall be called "Minister Monsters", and this Bill is intended to create those Ministers.
The amendments which have been proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), is to restore the designations which they ought to have since they are not really in charge of a full Department. They should continue to be called, for example, "Minister of State for International Trade". That eliminates the brackets. At least it does that, Mr. Speaker. I commend the Hon. Member for bringing forward an amendment which would eliminate those brackets, as they appear in the list of Ministries in the Wednesday Hansard. The same applies to Motion No. 3, "The Minister of State for", and again Motion No. 7, "the Minister of State for International Trade". There are three Ministers in one Department and it is described in subsequent clauses of the legislation that the "Minister" shall do this, and the "Minister" shall do that. It says in Part 1(2):
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (in this Part referred to as the "Minister")
Now they are introducing two additional Ministers in that section. Perhaps the best way to categorize this legislation is that it is very sloppily drafted. It bears all the marks of an organizational whiz-kid who decides that he wants to reshuffle matters, possibly to the satisfaction of the recipients of those titles, so that they may satisfy their egos that they are indeed Ministers and not just Ministers of State.
I do not know whether one Minister or the other was instrumental in ensuring that this Bill was drafted and brought forward in its present form. However, I believe if we were to look at the table of precedents in the most recent Wednesday's Hansard, we would find that there are in fact nine Ministers of State responsible for a variety of different areas of Government; External Relations, the Canadian Wheat Board, International Trade, Economic Development, Science and Technology, Multiculturalism, Fitness and Amateur Sports, Small Business and Tourism, and Finance. Are we going to be faced, Mr. Speaker, in the days to come, with the requirement that all these Ministers of State, some of whom have Departments under their jurisdiction, some of whom have not, will be required to be called, for example, Minister for Fitness and Amateur Sports? The Minister of State for Finance will be in some difficulty because we already have one Minister of Finance, and that, Mr. Speaker, if I may suggest, is quite enough.
I do find it odd that we should today be debating this particular matter. Incidentally, I should add that a little advance notice on this would have helped. I had a number of notes on the reorganization proposals for the Department of External Affairs which I had hoped to be able to use in any discussion in the House on this particular Bill. I find, however, that those notes have somehow or other disappeared with a lot of other papers and have become mislaid. Consequently, I am not able to focus on these amendments to the extent I feel they deserve.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, we cannot have a threeheaded Department of Government. I think we are asking for trouble. I think we should decide now to accept the amendments, and I do hope that Members on the other side will
October 24, 1983

consider the disputes which can arise as to jurisdiction within that Department. At one time, 1 believe, members of that Department could hold up their heads with pride at the job they were doing. Now, unfortunately, I have to say that altogether too many of them are just waiting for the day of their retirement. They are putting in their time, and that is a dreadful thing to have to say about public servants. They are not putting in that energy, that professionalism for which they have spent many years in training, into that particular Department. They are having to juggle themselves and rearrange themselves and unfortunately, 1 must admit, jockey for positions within that Department rather than attend to the matters to which they originally, with a great degree of dedication, were prepared to commit themselves to serve Canada both at home and abroad.
In support of my contention that they are having to jockey for position, I would suggest to you that some of the most highly trained, some of those with the greatest of experience, are serving at home because they find that the possibilities of getting along in the Department are much more likely to occur if they are within the range of one or other of these Ministers-it used to be just one. Now they will have to deal with three Ministers to make sure they have jockeyed in the right direction.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do urge upon Hon. Members opposite that they consider most seriously the amendments which have been put forward by my colleague, and that when the time comes to vote on these amendments, they will vote in favour.

Mr. Speaker, this deals with with position of the Minister for External Relations. In committee an amendment was introduced by the Government where, in Clause 9(2) the deputy minister shall be known as the deputy minister for political affairs. I do not know how many more types of affairs we are going to have but we have a Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), a Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), and his deputy minister for political affairs. I know I am facing up to the Government in its monolithic thinking where the Cabinet has said that this is going to be and the voices line up behind it. We have had the explanation for the creation of a Minister for International Trade. That takes the Trade out of Industry, Trade and Commerce and of course the Industry part is going over to a Minister of Industrial Development, and Commerce just dies. Except that, initially, the Commerce part dealt with business in Canada, but somewhere along the line no continuing emphasis has been maintained in that connection.
As I explained on Motion No. 1 which dealt with international trade, we have in this particular instance a Minister whose duties could quite conceivably be discharged by an efficient Parliamentary Secretary, in fact, a second Parliamentary Secretary if the Minister is so over-loaded due to the indolent nature of the Minister. We know he is not the most active and energetic of men, a man who rather than face up to an issue will duck out and not appear. This we have seen time and time again when he was the Minister of Finance and in other capacities. I have known him for 20 years as a Minister and frankly that has been one of the characteristics of his administration. So I do not see the necessity for having these Ministers, and quite clearly, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) said, these appointees are being given a title so that in the foreign pecking order they shall rank in title as full Ministers.
Then we have the Minister for External Relations. Well, if you did not know the difference, you might think he was the Secretary of State for External Affairs. But on the international level there is that ultimate pecking order and that is what
we are being asked to look after in this particular amendment. In addition to which we are raising his title to that of a Minister under Section 4 of the Salaries Act so that he may be paid not only his salary as Minister but he shall be entitled to a Parliamentary Secretary. You see, Section 5 of the Salaries Act, Mr. Speaker, covers Ministers of State. Ministers of State who do not have as a specific assignment a section of a Department are not entitled to a Parliamentary Secretary. For example, the Minister of State who is responsible for financial institutions is not entitled to a Parliamentary Secretary. This particular appointee is being classified as a Minister for External Affairs so that he may have a Parliamentary Secretary. This Bill could become popularly known as the financial emancipation of the Liberal backbenchers Bill because it creates a maximum of five more Parliamentary Secretaries.
Section 25 of the Bill will allow for some Parliamentary Secretaries to be named in the other place because, apparently, somebody must be able to reply there beyond the two or three Ministers who are there already, none of whom have any departmental responsibilities. I suppose therefore that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would like to have a nominee Parliamentary Secretary in the other place. Perhaps the Minister of State for External Affairs might like one as well.
I know that there will be two or possibly three Parliamentary Secretaries created by this particular Bill. I would like to reserve my argument on that, Mr. Speaker, until we get to the appropriate section. That is the only reason for the provisions of this Bill. They are purely cosmetic and will not improve the operations of the Department one jot or tittle. The Department of External Affairs will not be improved one iota by reason of the possible appointment of a Minister who will be called a Minister for External Relations.
Under the Ministries and Ministers of State Act there is already the power to appoint a Minister of State. This new Act allows for the appointment of a Minister for External Relations. He will be present in full cutaway coat and striped trousers if need be. That along with the creation of more Parliamentary Secretaries is the purpose of this Bill. Of course, the creation of more Parliamentary Secretaries is within the discretion of the patronage of the Liberal backbench. In the maximum of two years that it takes to rotate the Liberal backbench, somebody somewhere will have been able to collect something during that time.
There are presently 35 Ministers. There were 36 Ministers until one appointment went off like a damp squid. There are 27 Parliamentary Secretaries. There is now the potential for another five Parliamentary Secretaries. So the score in the football game will become that much closer. It will only be 35 to 32.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, if I could see something in these provisions which would improve the Department of External Affairs, I would agree with them. However, there is already a Minister of State, and my amendment proposes that
