subtopic: GARNISHEE, ATTACHMENT AND PENSION DIVERSION ACT- DELAY IN PROCLAMATION. (B) SOURCE OF OBJECTIONS TO PROCLAMATION
GARNISHEE, ATTACHMENT AND PENSION DIVERSION ACT- DELAY IN PROCLAMATION. (B) SOURCE OF OBJECTIONS TO PROCLAMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 16, 1983, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan) a question concerning a delay in proclaiming Bill C-38. I now rise to participate in this adjournment debate because I find myself shocked and distressed at the treatment Bill C-38 has received since it was passed by the House on June 18, 1982. It is a year and a half since this House passed the Bill and it has not yet been proclaimed in all parts.

October 24, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The Minister said in his answer, and quite truthfully, that the handling of this Bill was a "spectacle which might be considered rather unedifying for the people of the country." I am not certain that many people in the country are aware of this Bill. It mainly affects single parent families whom I do not expect have much time to watch the procedures of this House and look for this legislation. 1 would assume that the Minister responsible for the status of women is totally unaware of the effect the delay in proclaiming this Bill has on a very large group of women.
Part I of the Bill was proclaimed and is not part of my objection. Parts II, III and IV have not yet been proclaimed and consequently are not in effect after 17 months.
Let me read the title of the Bill so that Members will understand what I am talking about. Bill C-38 is:
An Act to provide for the garnishment or attachment of Her Majesty in right of Canada and for the diversion of pension benefits payable by Her Majesty in right of Canada under certain enactments.
The final paragraph of the Bill deals with proclamation. Clause 56 states:
(1)	Part I shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation.
(2)	Parts II, ill and IV shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation.
I am particularly concerned that Part II, which deals with diversion of pension benefits to satisfy financial support orders, has not been proclaimed 17 months after it passed.
In general terms, Part II provides for the diversion of pensions to provide enforcement of financial support orders against pension benefits payable pursuant to the Superannuation Acts and like enactments referred to in the Schedule.
After waiting several months for Parliament's will to be done, I began to ask questions regarding this Bill. I believe I questioned the former Minister of National Defence on this matter at five or six consecutive meetings of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. It became apparent that a stall was being imposed on Parliament by its own bureaucracy.
In response to one of my inquiries, I received a copy of a memorandum sent to the Minister of Justice on June 20, 1983, which said:
Part II dealing with pension diversion is to be proclaimed at some point in the future. No time has been set for proclamation because of the need to iron out technical problems relating to the pensions of MPs and Senators.
That was signed by a departmental assistant in the Department of Justice. In all my inquiries about this Bill and its proclamation, I have never found a Senator or MP who questioned this Bill. In fact, they were quite unanimous in support of the Bill when it was before Parliament.
Another example of the attitude taken of Parliament by the bureaucracy in the case of this Bill is contained in a letter which the Minister of National Defence sent to me in reply to a question as to why a court order diverting 50 per cent of an annuity had been paid at a fixed dollar amount instead of rising with the indexation of the pension. The Minister of National Defence stated:
The legal advisors are of the opinion that 'Armed Forces pension income' refers to the CFSA annuity only and does not apply to any increase payable under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act.
Part II of Bill C-38, which has not been proclaimed, indicates at page 9 that "pension benefit" in subparagraph (g) "includes any benefit payable under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act or the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act in respect of that pension, annual allowance or annuity." In other words, it means that indexation will be applied to the payments made to the families.
The case before the courts which the Minister mentioned concerns only Part I of the Bill which has been proclaimed, garnishment of wages. I cannot see any reason a court action concerning garnishment should be used as an excuse for continuing delays in proclaiming Parts II, III and IV which deal with diversion of pensions to satisfy court orders for family support. It is quite different than garnishment of wages.
Members of Parliament knew what they were doing when they passed this Bill divesting themselves of an archaic financial self-protection device which was neither suitable nor equitable in this day and age. The Senators and the Crown agree, and what we have been faced with is a monumental affront to Parliament in this continuing war between democracy and bureaucracy.

subtopic: FINANCE-TRUST COMPANIES' RESTRICTIONS ON RENEWAL OF MORTGAGES. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO ASSIST HOME OWNERS. (C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
FINANCE-TRUST COMPANIES' RESTRICTIONS ON RENEWAL OF MORTGAGES. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO ASSIST HOME OWNERS. (C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 14, as reported at pages 28027 and 28028 of Hansard, I asked questions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) regarding the Interest Act and the fact that some trust companies and others were including a clause in their mortgage renewal loan agreements which required applicants for mortgage loans to waive their rights under Section 10 of the Interest Act.
I should like to quote from a current mortgage document. It reads:
You expressly waive any right of prepayment you now have or hereinafter may have pursuant to Section 10 of the Interest Act (Canada) and/or any similar federal or provincial legislation permitting prepayment prior to the maturity date of the loan agreement.
The Government of Canada, in its wisdom, caused to be passed an Act entitled the Interest Act. That Act gives a right to a mortgagor who wants to prepay a mortgage. The Provinces of Ontario and Manitoba have passed similar legislation which gives rights of prepayment to a mortgagor. The essence of Section 10 is that one may prepay a mortgage which has a five-year or longer term upon the payment of three months of interest penalty.
It now appears that a federally-chartered trust company can write into a contract a clause which strips the rights given a home owner or mortgagor under legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures of Ontario and Manitoba. I say that this is wrong. No corporation or other organization should be allowed to take from a citizen of Canada a statutory right passed by the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the Provinces and Territories.
Further, there was an action before the Supreme Court of British Columbia that dealt with the five-year period set down in Section 10 of the Interest Act. An insurance company claimed that the mortgage date for determining the five-year period set forth in Section 10 was the date of the Mortgage Renewal Agreement. By that strange logic you would never be able to exercise your rights under Section 10. By juggling the renewal date, they could arrange it so that the five-year anniversary date would never occur.
The B.C. Supreme Court ruled that the effective date of the mortgage for purposes of calculating the five-year period was not the renewal date, but rather the date the original mortgage document was signed.
To counter the ruling of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, some trust companies are adding a sentence that reads "The original mortgage is deemed to be dated as of the maturity date of the existing loan". This sets aside the ruling of the Supreme Court of British Columbia. There was no challenge to the ruling of the court. No appeal was launched. They merely added 17 words to a mortgage renewal document that sets aside the ruling of the court.
Adjournment Debate
Where is this leading us? Is the Government and Parliament going to allow a handful of trust companies to write into their contracts provisions that take from one party in the contract a right of prepayment set forth in federal and provincial statutes? Is this what Canada is all about? Are trust companies above the law? Can they, by adding a clause to a mortgage contract, set aside the decision of the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the Provinces of Canada as expressed in statutes passed by those bodies?
Any commercial or private contract, mortgage, or other instrument that, through its languages, expressly removes a right given to one party in a contract by federal or provincial statute should be prohibited by law.
It is no defence to say the matter would be defeated in a court of law. That view only compounds the seriousness of the actions of some trust companies. It smacks of manipulation of the law, for it says that if you, the mortgagor, have the time and the money, you can pursue a decision through the court and thus exercise your right under the Interest Act. Otherwise, you are bound by the terms of the contract even though they may be declared void by an action in a court of law.
We are not dealing here with a corporation with resources. We are dealing with a home owner who has a mortgage, the interest rate of which has been increased, putting financial stress on the home owner. You may wish to argue that the financial condition of the plaintiff is of no concern to the court. Whatever your argument, it should not be lawful for a corporation or anyone to cause one party to a contract to be stripped of his or her rights in that contract.
There are those who would have you believe that a contract is a contract and the matter ends there. In fact, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) has said as much; at the same time expressing her concern for the mortgagor.
Again, this is no defence for the trust company. We have written proof that the waiving of rights under Section 10 of the Interest Act was not discussed with prospective mortgagors. The addition of an interest differential charge was not discussed during the mortgage negotiations. In other words, most of the mortgage negotiations between some of the trust companies and the home owner seeking a mortgage were less than truthful.
We did have The Trust Companies Association before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. They were able to respond to a question on this subject, but the Chairman of the committee ruled that we must pursue other matters as The Trust Companies Association was before the committee on another subject.
We must continue to ask questions and take part in these debates and bring this matter to the attention of Parliament. Sometimes I wonder if anyone is listening out there, if anyone really gives a darn or if this matter will be frustrated along until, through the passage of time, the mortgages will run to term and the trust companies involved will have been successful in the largest rip-off in our history.

October 24, 1983
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-TRUST COMPANIES' RESTRICTIONS ON RENEWAL OF MORTGAGES. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO ASSIST HOME OWNERS. (C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Elon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) certainly shares with me and the Government considerable concern on this particular issue. I personally welcome the inquiries he has made and the initiative he has taken on this, and the opportunity he has given us to discuss government action and future courses of action.
I was with the Hon. Member on the Finance Committee when we deliberately raised this with the trust companies. I think he heard, as I did, that this is really a balancing act that we are trying to get across. On the one hand, as he pointed out very articulately, we have a problem with potential fraud or at least misleading innocent home owners. On the other hand we do not want to solve those specific cases by ruining the whole mortgage market. The Hon. Member knows that full well.
What has the Government done in this regard? First of all, 1 would remind him of the ongoing operation of the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan. I personally helped one of my own constituents to get a $3,000 grant under this scheme to lower the impact of the mortgage payments on their family income. That grant still stands. It is a good safety valve for individual home owners.
Second, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) indicated that she has the director of investigations and research checking, under the Combines Investigation Act, whether some kind of criminal or misleading behaviour has taken place.
Third, the Government has made it clear that it wants to review the Canada Interest Act to strengthen its provisions in order to avoid these kinds of misleading operations in the future.
Finally, we must remind all Canadians that they are signing a contract; that they are binding themselves.
I understand that there were about 750,000 people who took out high interest rate mortgages during the real crisis period of 1981 and 1982. Of those, we estimate that approximately 80 per cent or 600,000 took short-term mortgages, and that those people are seeing their problem solved now because mortgage rates have dropped so dramatically.
As for the other people, the vast majority knew what they were doing. They wanted the security of a four or five-year mortgage and they undertook that deliberately. The balance are people whose cases we have to investigate without destroying the whole mortgage market, but without allowing improper or misleading practices to continue I join the Hon. Member for Burlington in his concern about this issue.

ENERGY-RADIOACTIVE LAND FILL IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 23 I rose in the House to ask a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) regarding a land swindle that took place in Surrey in
1975. A constituent of mine innocently bought some valuable commercial property for his business only to find out later that the land fill on that property was material brought in from outside British Columbia which contained low level radioactive thorium, with the result that everyone in the surrounding area, and certainly the employees of the company working there, are very concerned about the exposure they face from that low level radiation. It may be that there is no immediate health danger, buit it may be that there is.
I have been working on this problem since 1978. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I have a letter dated September 2, 1978, from the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, one Mr. Alastair Gillespie of "coalgate" fame.

speechtext:
He states, in the last paragraph of his letter: "I have asked the AECB to give priority consideration to the resolution of this matter in the interest of the concerns of the Surrey community". That was in 1978. If that is the speed with which this Government operates it is no wonder the country is in the mess it is in. At the time I did not know the interrelationship of that particular swindle.
A former Member of Parliament of the Liberal Government, one Mark Smerchanski from southern Manitoba, owned a company called Fundy Chemical. He represented southern Manitoba from 1968 to 1972, but was defeated in the 1972 election. Knowing what he was doing, he foisted that polluted land onto an innocent customer. As soon as the customer found out what he had bought he took Mr. Smerchanski to court. At the beginning of the court proceedings Mr. Smerchanski had $250,000 in a Fundy Chemical account, but by the time proceedings were finished the account was bone dry with the result that the company received nothing and is still waiting. Even though the customer won an $800,000 settlement, he has received nothing from Mr. Smerchanski.
I ask the Government whether it understands the kind of financial implication this has for a company? Does it realize that all the financial structure of a company like this is based on the value of its property? If that property is worth $800,000, or $1 million, according to the court's settlement, and he takes the value of that property to the bank as collateral for a loan and the bank realizes the land is virtually valueless because it is contaminated, how much would the bank give him? The whole financial structure of the company is raped because this one man violated a sense of trust with a customer.
Is the Government taking all these years to deal with the problem because it has a cozy relationship with Mr. Smerchanski and does not want to contaminate that relationship? Is the government slow in acting because it does not know what to do with the material or because it does not care? Is the Government pursuing options in British Columbia as a result of the possibility of a new site for this kind of material being found in the general area of Ashcroft. Does the Minister realize what this has done to the financial picture of this
October 24, 1983

company? Does he realize at all what it means to a company like this in terms of its financial future?
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary if we can expect an immediate resolution of this problem so that the employees working on the site can expect to work in safety. Will the Government underwrite soil removal on that land fill site so that employees are not in danger? For example, would the Government get different property for this company so that it does not have to bear the cost of having semi valueless property? Will it remove all that material to a site that will contain radioactivity, and thereby remove any threat to the health of the people of British Columbia, and particularly of Surrey? What kind of financial support will the Government underwrite for a constituent who has been violated by a former member of the Government and needs some kind of recourse to restore the health of his company?

Mr. Speaker, 1 have always had a good deal of respect for the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), but I must say I am a little disappointed that the case he advocates today is so full of innuendo.

Members that the low level radioactive waste at Surrey B.C. is the result of the importation and processing of a metallurgical ore in 1972. The resulting 350 tonnes of slag was on the Anvil Way property of Fundy Chemicals when it was bought by Comor Supplies in 1975. The import licence for the ore material included a requirement to obtain AECB approval before disposal.
The new owner was informed of the radioactive content of the slag by an AECB inspector in 1976 and has since successfully prosecuted the former owner for fraud. The latest judgment, which was for $642,000 from the B.C. Supreme Court
Adjournment Debate
in August 1982, was based on the cost of cleanup and removal of the wastes from the Anvil Way site. The new proprietor has also introduced a court action against the AECB and the B.C. Ministry of the Environment which, if successful, would require that a site be found for the waste. The federal Government is now actively co-operating with the B.C. Government in trying to resolve this problem once and for all.
However, the Hon. Member asked if the Government of Canada was doing anything or was concerned about low level radioactive waste. I wish to inform him that a Low Level Radioactive Waste Management Office under AECL has been set in motion and that office, Mr. Speaker, has two main objectives. The first is to undertake those studies and actions necessary to resolve historic waste problems which are the responsibility of the federal Government. Historic wastes are those which have been managed in a manner no longer considered satisfactory and for which the original producer cannot reasonably be held responsible. The historic wastes consist mainly of soil contaminated with radium and uranium and were formerly the responsibility of the Federal-Provincial Task Force on Radioactivity. The second objective is to establish or arrange for the establishment of a waste management collection and disposal service which can be used by appropriate producers and users of radio isotopes on a fee for service basis.
I am pleased to say that since the formation of this office considerable progress has been made with the co-operation of the provincial governments. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that in the coming months and, indeed, the coming years, this matter will be resolved, not only to the satisfaction of the residents of the Hon. Member's constituency, but also to the satisfaction of Members of Parliament.
